Mr. CLEMENTS-by Mr. Sproule-asked:
1.	How many inspectors or veterinary surgeons have been employed by the government for the years 1902, 1903 and 1904, for the prevention of hog disease, or other animal disease in West Kent ?
2.	Who were the officials, and who are engaged at the present time ?
3.	What salaries were paid to each, and what is paid at the present time ?
4.	Does the government intend keeping present officials retained at present salaries ?
5.	If that said disease, known as hog plague, has abated in the said county, what are the duties of above officials ; and are they allowed expenses outside of present' salaries ?

1.	In the year 1902, three veterinary inspectors were employed. In 1903-4, the number was increased to 5, while at the present time, 4 officers are engaged in dealing with animal diseases in West Kent and adjoining territory.
2.	In 1902 the only resident officer was Dr. J. Kime, jr., V.S., of Chatham, but in Ibe latter part of the year, owing to an extensive outbreak of hog cholera, it became necessary to transfer to the district, Dr. M. B. Perdue, V.S., formerly of Kingsville, Dr. G. W. Orchard, V.S., of Windsor, and Dr. J. H. Tennent, V.S., of London.
In 1903 the officers engaged in the work were Drs. Perdue, Orchard, Kime, and for a short time, Drs. Hopkins and Whyte of Ottawa. Towards the end of the year, Dr. W. B. Rowe of Blenheim, and Dr. M. Philips of Chatham were also engaged.
In 1904, Drs. Perdue, Orchard, Philips, Kime and Rowe looked after the work without outside assistance. Dr. Orchard has recently been removed, and the staff at present consists of Drs. Perdue, Kime, Rowe and Philips.
3.	1902. Dr. Perdue, 8 months at $75, 4 months at $100. Dr. Kime, $650. Dr. Orchard, $500 p. a.
1903.	Dr. Perdue, $1,200 p.a. Dr. Kime, $250 p. a. Dr. Orchard, 3 months at $500, 9 months at $1,000. Dr. Rowe, 3 months at $250 p. a. Dr. Philips, 1 month at $600 p. a.
1904.	Dr. Perdue, 3 months at $1,200, 9 months at $1,400. Dr. Kime, $250 p. a. Dr. Orchard, $1,000 p. a. Dr. Rowe, $250 p. a. Dr. Philips, 6 months at $600, 6 months at $800.
Present staff : Dr. Perdue, $1,400 p. a. Dr. Kime, $250 p. a. Dr. Rowe, $250 p. a. Dr. Philips, $800 p. a.
Drs. Tennent and Whyte, both permanent officers of the department, were in receipt of salaries of $1,200 p. a.
Drs. Kime and Rowe, being resident practitioners, are paid $250 per annum, with an allowance of $5 per day for each day above fifty, in which they are employed by the department in any one year.
4.	The policy of the department* is to maintain within the quarantined area a sufficient number of officials to deal in an effective manner with outbreaks of disease.
5.	Although the disease has abated to a considerable extent, the outbreak is by no means at an end, fresh cases still being reported, though not to so large an extent as formerly. The district is still under quarantine, and all hogs are inspected and passed,

under permit, by one of our inspectors before being allowed to leave the infected area. The inspectors also deal with outbreaks of ether contagious disease in animals.
There are also a large number of farms still under quarantine, the necessary cleansing and disinfection not having been yet completed.
All the inspectors at present employed in West Kent are allowed their actual travelling expenses.

Mr, LAKE asked :
1.	What are the lands referred to In the speech of the Prime Minister on the 22nd instant, Hansard, page 1518, as follows :-' Or if the price of government lands for sale were to be increased over the present very moderate, &c.' ?
2.	At what price are these lands offered for sale, and under what terms and conditions ?
3.	Are they open to purchase by any applicant who applies for them ?
Right Hon. Sir WIlFRID LAURIER (Prime Minister).
1.	Ordinary Dominion Lands in Manitoba and the Northwest Territories which were sold at the rate of $3 per acre.
2.	$3 per acre was the price [DOT] fixed by Order in Council ; but the lands are not offered for sale, but sold to settlers only.
3.	No.

In reference to that question which the right hon. Prime Minister has answered does he know just at present whether such lands on sale at ?3 per acre are open to all applicants who are settlers or all who are applicants ?
No, except where it would be a special hardship to refuse an application.
Such have to come before the minister to determine whether it is a case of that kind or not ?
I do not know that.

Mr. Speaker, before the Orders of the Day are called I would like to call the attention of the government to a paragraph that appeared in yesterday's ' Citizen ' to the following effect:
Admiral Freemantl^ presided at a meeting at which was placed before the Southwark ratepayers Mrs. Gloses' scheme for the emigration of pauper children to Nova Scotia. It was explained that the Canadian government, Lord Minto and the Duke of Argyle all favour the scheme, which furthermore would he a great pecuniary saving to the ratepayers.
I may say that there has been a good deal iu the papers about the kind of immigrants who are coming to the cities and town of this country. Some of the benevolent associations have been taxed to their full capacity and a little more to provide for them during the winter, and I hope there is nothing in this paragraph because I do not think this would be a desirable kind of immigration for us to bring to Canada.
Would the hon. gentleman send me the information that he has and I will give him an answer to-morrow ?

I may say that I sent the right hon. gentleman yesterday a notice of this matter and I inclosed a clipping from the ' Citizen.'
^Sir WILFRID LAURIER. My hon. friend told me that he was going to bring the matter up on going into Committee of Supply. The House will be going into Committee of Supply shortly.

I saw the ex-Minister of the Interior (Mr. Sifton) outside afterwards and he said he would inform the right hon. First Minister and that he would much prefer that the matter be brought on the Orders of the Day saying that he himself would answer it.
I will send over to the hon. gentleman the information placed in my hands.

Mr. Speaker, before the Orders of Day are called I wish to refer to a matter of considerable importance to my own province of Ontario and to put myself in order I intend to conclude with a motion. The matter to which I purpose calling the attention of the House is the somewhat equivocal position occupied by the hon. member for London (Mr. Hyman) in this House. Ever since the last general election the hon. Minister of Public Works (Mr. Sutherland), who sat in this House for North Oxford, has not

been here. I understand that he is very ill. I am sorry to know it. I have a great respect for that hon. gentleman and I believe he enjoys the respect of every one in this House, but in strenuous times like these we have a constitutional practice to uphold, and I do not think the position occupied at the present moment by the hon. member for London as acting Minister of Public Works is quite within the constitution. Nay, I will go further and say that I believe that the hon. member for North Oxford has already placed his resignation as Minister of Public Works in the hands of the right hon. gentleman who leads the government (Sir Wilfrid Laurier). Probably he may have in his pocket to-day the resignation of that hon. gentleman but, at all events if he be ill-and I am sorry to say that he is ill- in times like these I say that if we are to respect the constitutional practice it is the duty either of the hon. member for North Oxford to resign his position as Minister of Public Works or it is the duty of the right hon. Prime Minister to ask for that resignation. and if he desires the hon. member for London to fill that position the constitution requires that that hon. gentleman shall go back to his constituents for their endors-ation. My object in calling attention to this condition of affairs is that matters of high policy are before the people of Canada today and a splendid opportunity is presented to test public feeling on these questions. If the right, hon. gentleman has confidence in his policy ; if he has confidence in his great majority-I would ask him what his majority is ?
Seventy.

I understand it is over sixty if there have not been some defections within the last day or two. Be that as it may the constitutional practice requires that the man who is filling the [DOT]portfolio of Public Works should enjoy the confidence of his constituents and be reelected. If the Prime Minister has the resignation of Mr. Sutherland in his pocket he ought to make the country aware of it. It is putting the hon. member for London (Mr. Hyman) in an anomalous position. Then there is another thing; the man who does the work is entitled to the pay, and if the member for London does the work he ought to draw the salary. As a man from the province of Ontario, I am anxious to see our cabinet ministers occupy their positions in good standing, and I do not wish it to be pointed out that a minister from that great province is declasse in the cabinet. Let him have all the honours he is entitled to and let him have them in a constitutional way. I believe the Prime Minister is possibly in a position to declare that the seat for North Oxford is vacant, and at the same time he is in a position to declare that the seat for London shall be
made vacant. Perhaps my hon. friend from London (Mr. Hyman) would prefer to run in North Oxford, but I do not care particularly about that so long as he has the endorsement of the people of his own province and his own neighbourhood who ought to be permitted to pass judgment upon him and upon those with whom he is associated in the government. I beg to move that the House do now adjourn.

My hon. friend (Mr. Maclean) is getting into the habit of moving the adjournment of the House daily. If he finds some pleasure in that nobody can find any very great displeasure, and I do not think it concerns the House very much that he should continue to pursue such a course. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Maclean) says that if I had in my pocket the resignation of the member for North Oxford (Hon. Mr. Sutherland) it is my duty to give it to the House. The hon. gentleman is quite right in that; it is the only thing in which I can agree with him. For once, I congratulate him on being correct in his law if not in his facts. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Maclean) stated that he had reason to believe that I had such resignation in my pocket. I would be glad to know where the hon. gentleman has obtained such information. I do not think he will venture to give it to the House, and if he does I shall afford him an opportunity of doing so.
I will tell the right hou. gentleman what I think.

Oh, no; I want my hon. friend to tell me where he got the information that at this moment I have in my pocket the resignation of the Minister of Public AVorks. I think I know his source of information, and I think it is to be found in the fertile imagination of the hon. gentleman from South York. I am afraid there is no other source than that, because as a matter of fact I have not the resignation of my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works. He has never offered it to me. If the Minister of Public Works had offered me his resignation simply because his health was not good. I can tell the hon. gentleman from South York that I would have asked the Minister of Public Works to keep his resignation back.
Hear, hear.

I would have told the Minister of Public Works that members on both sides of the House, with one single exception, would be glad to know that there was hope that he would take his place again in this House as Minister of Public AArorks. My hon. friend the Minister of Public Works has not offered me his resignation and I am very thankful that he has not. One observation more; the

hon. gentleman (Mr. Maclean) says that the hon. member for London (Mr. Hyman) who is acting as minister ought to have the pay -well, apparently that question does not trouble my hon. friend from London (Mr. Hyman) and I cannot see why it should trouble my hon. friend from York (Mr. Maclean).
The Prime Minister has two great weaknesses ; he has the weakness of making the effort of his life and he has the weakness when violating the constitution to take refuge- in personal friendships.
Oh, oh.

Hon gentlemen opposite may jeer, but what are the facts ? It is all very fine to say that we have a constitution, but if we have we ought to respect it. We ought not to be constantly violating it, because it suits party considerations, and because the Prime Minister is afraid to test public opinion in the province of Ontario. That's what's the matter. It is very nice to hear about personal honour and about regard for an hon. minister who happens to be ill, but there are more than personal matters to be considered in the conduct of public business. We want a Minister of Public Works who has the endorsation of his constituents, and that we have not. We do not know how long we may be without such a minister, and though that may be the Prime Minister's view of the constitution it is not the view of the constitution that obtains in England.
My hon. friend is wrong there.

The right hon. gentleman asks me how I know that he has in his pocket the resignation of the hon. member for North Oxford. Well, I believe that the hon. member from North Oxford from a sense of honour and responsibility to the public, would have long since placed his resignation in the hands of his leader. I leave the case there and I say that the present state of affairs is not satisfactory and ought to be corrected. I hope yet to bring the Prime Minister to my way of thinking on this matter. He is not above changing his mind; I believe that since yesterday a wonderful change has come over his mind and perhaps over his heart as well, and that we will see a very pronounced modification of the policy which he announced the other day. I have the greatest respect for the acting Minister of Public Works (Mr. Hyman); I meet him every day and I am glad to meet him, but I would like to see him in this House enjoying all the honours he is entitled to. I trust that the Prime Minister will give the hon. member for London (Mr. Hyman) his full dignity Sir WILFRID LAURIER.
and at the same time maintain the principles of the constitution.
Motion to adjourn, negatived.
SUPPLY.	'
House in Committee of Supply.
Intercolonial Railway-diversion of line at Mitchell, $15,000.

This is a revote. By the 1st of July next we shall have expended about $10,000 of the vote of $25,000 made last session. There is at that point a very bad curve of seven degrees which it is proposed to bring down to two degrees. There is also a bridge, which it is proposed to replace.
Where is Mitchell ?
It is on the Drummond Counties line.
What is the work supposed to cost altogether ?
$25,000. The contract for grading is $12,000, and the rest of the amount covers land damages for right of way, the cost of the permanent way, ballasting, changing the telegraph line, and so on.
How much of a diversion does it make from the main line ?
The present line is 8,740 feet in length, and it will be reduced by 1.237 feet. The grade will also be reduced to four-tenths.
There is also a diversion of the line at St. Leonard Junction. Is that on the same line ?
Yes.
What is the reduction there in length, in curve and in grade ?

We reduce the curve from five to two degrees, the grade to about eight-tenths, and the distance about 128 feet in 5,850 feet. We do not make the diversion in order to shorten the distance, but in order to reduce the grade and the curve.
Are there any other diversions on the Drummond line ?
These are the only two, I think.
How far is this curve from the bridge ?
Both the curve at Mitchell and the curve at St. Leonard Junction are near the bridges.
Does the change involve raising the grade of the bridge at the other end ?
I can show the hon. gentlemen a plan, which was here last session. The bridge as located was too low, and it was necessary to raise it anyway.
This curve is partly in the county of Drummond and partly in Ni-colet. It is in the form of an 'S' and a really bad curve.
Are there many such curves on that road ?
The minister says there are only two.
I suppose there will be many more at the next election.
This was voted long before the election ; there are no votes there.

Has any separate account been kept as to what was spent on the Drummond County line since the government took it over ? I think the House is entitled to that information and it should be kept separately.
There has been no special account; I do not think the amount has been very large in the main. This change is one of the largest made in connection with this road.

Would the minister be good enough to tell the committee the difference in the location of the old bridge and the new bridge that he proposes to build ? How far will the new bridge be up the river from the old bridge ?
The plan will show that.

I fail to understand the position of the government in 1898 and its position to-day. In 1898, when this road was bought, it was stated in the House, time and time again, that it was a first-class road, it was a cheap road, and the government could not get along without buying it; they were buying a mint in buying that road. I have known that road for a very long time. When the road was first built it was a straight road without curves, and to-day it is a road with sharp and heavy curves. How was that done ? Would the minister explain that to me ? The minister was not in office at that time and I do not propose to charge him with false representations made at that time, but nevertheless they were made.

Two swallows do not make a summer nor do two curves on a road condemn the entire road. I think it certainly speaks well for the accuracy of the reprsentations made as regards that road that it has been found necessary to change only two curves on it. The Intercolonial Railway is recognized as one of the standard roads of Canada, and yet we find it necessary to correct curves on it. We are asking $60,000 to correct the curvature at Birch Cove the approach to the city of Halifax, and there are other curves and other grades on the Intercolonial Railway. But because of that you would not condemn the Intercolonial Railway; you would say that, generally speaking, it is one of the best roadways to be found in all Canada.
I agree to that, but as I said before that road was highly recommended in the House.
This does not condemn it.

There is a place, not far from that point called St. Germain, where the roadbed is overflowed for about 6 miles every year. The government, some years ago, had to put rails on the ties to keep the road from floating out. Then they raised the road about three feet. How does it come if the road was so good in 1898 that it has become bad since then ? The road then had light curves ; now it has heavy curves ; then it had good bridges, now you are taking bridges away and building others. What is the use of trying to blindfold people in that way ? I know very well that the road at that time was not even a second-class road. I understand what a good road is as well as any man in the House and that road, at that time, was not a second-class road, yet it was highly recommended, and to-day it has very much deteriorated. How can you account for that ?

The statement of the minister is correct. There is a great deal in his statement that the road must have been of an excellent character when it was necessary to take out only two curves. The House requires a little more authority than the bald statement of the minister in reference to that. If I am not mistaken a good many more improvements have been made, and as the hon. member for Dorchester (Mr. Morin) said when we were asked to take over that road, it was said to be a first-class road, capable of running on the same time schedules as the Intercolonial Railway. We paid $1,429,000 for it at the time and the minister of that day promised to keep the accounts separate just as he promised to keep a separate account of the Canada Eastern. The House is entitled to know from the minister what the expenditure on capital account on that road has been since it was purchased in 1898. Then we will be able to judge, outside of the mere statement of the minister, whether it has been found necessary to make only two improvements on the road. If I remember rightly when the road was taken over, there was a report from the Department of Railways and Canals in reference to the character of the road. The report from the department stated that there was one very heavy curve which it might be necessary to take out and to change the gradients on the ap-

proach to It. What amount of money have we expended on what has been alleged in the House was an entirely second-class road at the time of the purchase, and what expenditure have we made on capital account on that road up to the present day.

(Translation.) The hon. member for Dorchester (Mr. Morin) does not know what he is talking about when he says the government have added three feet to the roadbed at St. Germain. That statement is entirely inaccurate. Nothing was done but to extend the yard so as to devote more space to the traffic which has considerably increased since the purchase of the Drummond by the government. In reference to Mitchell, at that place there is a dangerous curve and the government does very well in rectifying the error made at the time of the establishment of that line. I think it is incumbent upon the engineers in charge of the Intercolonial to see to it so as to prevent the accidents that might occur at that particular place, instead of waiting any longer. Far from deserving any blame, the government are entitled to our congratulations on account of the wise measures taken. Moreover, we must bear in mind that the Drummond brings a good revenue to the Intercolonial. If there is a division which covers all its expenses and yields profits, it is that of the Drummond. We must not be stingy about the necessary repairs in order to better accommodate the traffic in that part of the country and to protect the lives of the travelling public.

Mr. Chairman, the hon. gentleman (Mr. D. Lavergue) has spoken in French. I could reply in French ; but I am going to reply in English. I have been talking about one thing and my hon. friend is talking about another. There it is. I stated to the House that the facts had been misrepresented in 1898, when the road was bought. That is what I said before, and that is what I say still. My hon. friend says that this place St. Germain is a grand place with a great traffic. I have not the least doubt about it ; and I do not say a word against St. Germain. I am only talking about what the government then told the House. They told us that this was a first-class road, and that by buying it we would give the government a great chance to make money. They told us : We are going to have a through road from Halifax to Montreal, and it will be a grand help to the road we have now. Well, where is the grand help to-day ? A deficit of a million dollars. How do you account for that ? It only shows that that side of the House tried to blindfold this side in 1898, and they are trying to do it to-day ; but they will not succeed. The proofs are there ; the words that were spoken are there. And the money has been paid out-$1,600,000. That is what I said before, and that is what Mr. HAGGART.
I say now ; and I do not take one word back.
Mr. OSLER, The hon. minister (Mr. Emmerson), replying to me a moment ago, said it would be easy to get these figures showing the capital expenditure in connection with the Drummond County road. Will the hon. gentleman kindly furnish the figures so that we may have them before the matter is taken up again ?

And I think that the minister, when bringing down that information, should bring down further information concerning which, no doubt, discussion will arise. It is possible for ministers to make statements in the House when bringing new schemes before parliament, which statements may not turn out to be true. Various reasons may be urged in excuse. But it is always an excellently good thing to sift these statements and promises made when a new scheme is brought before parliament and compare them with the actual results. That is what I think we ought to do now. We ought to know how far these statements made by the ministers when they were purchasing this road have been proven true. Now, not only were statements made with regard to the condition of the road- its grades and curves, and so on-but there was also a most important consideration in the way of traffic advantages that we were to gain from this purchase. Certainly parliament at that time would have taken a very different view of the question if they had been told that they were merely purchasing an extension for the Intercolonial Railway without any advantages in the way of interchange of freight and consequent increase of through traffic for the Intercolonial Railway. Statements were made as to the kind and amount of traffic that the Grand Trunk Railway were to hand over to the Intercolonial Railway, especially freight traffic. Has that forecast made by the ministry been realized ? Has that agreement been carried out ? I have had an opportunity to look over what is called the ' statement of the case ' before the arbitrators, whose labours, I imagine, are just now about finished, as to the points in dispute between the Grand Trunk and the Intercolonial. And there can be no stronger condemnation of the promises made and statements put forth by the Minister of Railways and other members of the government in support of the proposed purchase of this railway, than the statement of the government a few years later, as to the absolute non-fulfilment of the conditions that form a part of the consideration paid for in the purchase of that road. If these statements are true-and at least they embody the view of the government on the subject- the non-diversion of freights is established. As to whether the Grand Trunk Railway can be held in damages is another matter. But no one can read this ' statement of the

case ' and not be convinced that the results that were so rosily pictured and that were anticipated by the government, have not been realized. Consequently, the money of this country was paid for a consideration the country lias never received. We did get the road. It certainly was not a iirst-elass road. A large amount has been spent on capital account in order to make it a running road at all in connection with the Intercolonial Railway. That expense has to be borne. But we got none of the vast gathering of traffic from the west which was to be picked up by the Grand Trunk Railway system and handed over to the Intercolonial Railway. Instead of the promised delivery of traffic to our road, we have practically a systematic diversion of traffic carried out by the Grand Trunk, if the allegations of the government in these latter years are true- and I presume they are. Now, we must go into that question. We must hold the government responsible for the pretenses under which it makes a purchase with the people's money. We want to know exactly how their scheme has turned out. So I would like the minister to bring down a statement showing for each year wliat traffic has been transferred to the Intercolonial according to the agreements, we were told, had been made. Without going into details, the minister will know what we need, and will afford us such information on this subject as he has in his possession. My bon. friend (Mr. Emmersou) was not responsible for this purchase. I do not know whether he would have recommended it if he had been minister at that time. It is well, for his sake, as well as for ours, that we should know just how things have turned out up to this date, and how we stand with reference to the Drummond County road and this promised transfer of traffic.

The information asked for will be produced. I might say in this connection that the contract entered into in 1898 might very well have been a good contract, a justifiable contract, on the assumption that both parties to tlie agreement would carry out the promises made under it. I think parliament had a right to assume that the Grand Trunk Railway, in entering into a contract to do certain things, would, bona fide, fulfil their obligation. Upon that assumption, the contract could very well have been approved by parliament. And yet the contract may not have been fulfilled. The Grand Trunk may have failed to carry out its obligation in later years. That would not be a condemnation of the contract ; rather would it be a reflection upon one of the parties to the contract who had obligated themselves to do certain things and failed to do them. However, that is neither here nor there.
That will appear better when we get the information.
It can be discussed then, and we will be in a better position to-determine whether it has been fulfilled, either in the letter or in the spirit.

In reference to what the minister has just said, it was pointed. out from this side of the House in the strongest manner possible when that contract was made, that the obligation on the part of the Grand Trunk was an obligation in word only, and that there was absolutely no reason to suppose that the contract was binding on the Grand Trunk.
Lawyers differ.

But the government took no step whatever to try to make that contract more binding ; and if it has turned out as the opposition said it would, then the government are entirely to blame, as they knowingly entered into a contract with this grave defect in it.
'Wilfully and with malice afore thought.'

If the minister says that, I will accept it-that they wilfully entered irto a contract knowing there was a weakness on one side. It was not a bargain made between two parties who were anxious to effect a business transaction.
Increase ol accommodation at Moncton, $110,000.
Last year we voted $210,000, and we have expended $100,000 during the year, so this is a revote of $110,-C00.
How much altogether do j ou propose to expend down there ?

If it becomes necessary to build additions to the general offices at Moncton, the total, with what has been already expended, would amount to half a million dollars. That involves the enlargement of the machine shop and also erecting another shop, and putting a second story oa the car shop. There are quite a number of large items. It also involves the purchase of additional laud, some fifteen acres near the present station ; it is between the north line and the line which runs to St. John. We are much cramped for room, and besides are expecting the entry of the Grand Trunk Pacific into the city of Moncton, which will make it necessary for the Intercolonial to acquire some of that land. My bon. tiiend from Lanark (Mr. Haggart) who was Minister of Railways, must know that the purchase has been under consideration for some years, and now it will have to be effected.
What has been done to the general offices ?

If the work of the railway increases, there will have to be an-

other wing. Within two or three years we have furnished a third story. There is no elevator in the building. If it is not possible to add another story, we will have to build ar other wing. They are very much cramped for room now. I had an opportunity a few weeks ago of going through the building, and I certainly felt that, for sanitation purposes, the condition should not be allowed to continue-for that consideration alone, if for no other.
Bad drains ?	,
No, too many in a room.
I think that could be arranged without making any capital expenditure.

Perhaps my hon. friend means to intimate that we might dispense with some of the officials there ; it might be arranged in that way no doubt. But I think that is a proper capital expenditure on the road.

Would it not be better to face this matter at once ? We are year by year increasing the debt of the country, nominally, by increasing the capital expenditure on the Intercolonial. Let us wipe off the deficiency year by year and face it, else we will have a debt running up into a hundred millions, on only nominal assets of the country. We have been spending everything on this road out of capital, let us change the system so that the people may see exactly what it costs each year.

I think there are other railways besides the Intercolonial that have to make expenditures on capital account, and to do so they have to come to parliament for power to issue additional stock. Since I have been in this parliament, although it has been but a few years, I have seen great railway corporations of the country coming here and asking for power to make betterments on their roads, construction, and improvements of their terminals, and improvements in their offices and their buildings. I think it is not an unusual thing for railways to do that, and it is not to be condemned, if it is necessary, even on the Intercolonial.

The minister is quite right in that, but there is this difference, that these companies who come asking for power to increase their capital, have to go to the public to borrow it, and they could not borrow it unless they increased the capital to pay interest. But in this case there is no possibility that these expenditures are going to pay interest.
The minister is quite right in what he says. But while some companies come here asking for changes in their Acts of incorporation, others come here and sell their roads out and out to the government.
We have a sample in the Drummond County road and another in the Canada Eastern. Those people got rid of their roads, and got their money.
They say they lost money by it.

I would ask the minister if it is the intention of the government to provide a new station for Fredericton ? The station of the Canada Eastern in that city is entirely inadequate and unsuitable for a city of the importance of Fredericton. I may say also that the station of the Canadian Pacific Railway at Fredericton is not sufficient to meet the requirements of that community. I have heard it frequently suggested *that the matter should be taken up by the Minister of Railways with the Canadian Pacific Railway, to see if some agreement could not be arrived at by which a union station could be provided for that city. I call the attention of the Minister of Railways to this matter so that he may give it his consideration.

If my hon. friend will only square himself with my hon. friend who sits in front of him (Mr. Haggart), I think I may safely take that into consideration. But I do not want the "Canada Eastern to earn the title of being a sink hole for expenditure, as it was alleged to be by the hon. member for Lanark. The purchase of the Canada Eastern has been so recent that I have not had time to consider making any serious betterments. The station ttat was used in connection with it at Fredericton has been of some service I think, but I am not personally aware whether or not it meets the requirements of the traffic. Of course, all these things have to be taken into consideration in connection with the road. I have felt that the Canada Eastern must in a measure work out its own salvation, and if the traffic on that road and the conditions prevailing on it justify improvements, they will be provided. But I have not ascertained yet that there is any great necessity of the immediate construction of a new station at Fredericton.

Mr. Chairman, I think it is very easy to lay down the rule which has been adopted, and I think fairly well followed on the Intercolonial Railway. It is recognized by all railway authorities that any expenditure to the extent to which it is a betterment of the railway is a fair charge against capital account. The creation of something which has not heretofore existed, some work in connection with the road which is necessary for its successful operation, any improvement in the matter of appliances, that is some appliance which has not heretofore been in existence in connection with the railway, I think constitutes a proper charge against capital account-anything which is not in substitution of something else. There may be a necessity on the railway of replacing something that existed-there are modifications to that rule-but to a certain extent that is not chargeable to capital account.
To what extent ? Give an instance.

To the extent to which it is a non-existing improvement it may be chargeable to capital, but to the extent to which it is a substitution of something that has heretofore existed it will be fairly I think, a revenue charge. It is very difficult to define the exact line between the two.
For instance if the hon. gentleman were taking up 60-lb. rails and and putting down 90-lb. rails ?

There is a difference. There has been a special rule and it has been followed in connection with that. That
has been discussed in this House time and again. I am making a general statement as to the course which is followed. I think that when my hon. friends opposite were responsible for the Intercolonial Railway and since, there have been special expenditures chargeable to capital account which would not perhaps comply with the strict rule or come under the definition that I have referred to.

The remarks of my hon. friend from North Toronto (Mr. Foster) open up a very nice question as to what should be charged to capital and what to revenue account. An extravagant minister, a minister who is lavish in expenditures,-
That does not apply to me.

Not at all. There should be no capital account on the Intercolonial Railway from Montreal to Halifax or any portion of it as at present constituted. I am laying down a principle, not my own, but the principle of the leader of the Liberal government, Mr. Mackenzie, who contended that a capital account is only an excuse for bad management of the road. It is no use of making comparisons between the expenditures of one government and another. If a minister is allowed to charge things to capital account which otherwise will go into ordinary expenditures there is no limit to the extravagance which may take place. The idea of the hon. gentleman expending on a road which has been finished for nearly forty years a sum of money equal to nearly $4,000,000 a year for three or four years-
It is only 30 years really since the northern division was opened up to Riviere du Loup.
Part of it was finished before confederation.
I am speaking of the road, from Moncton to Riviere du Loup That was not opened up until 1875.

Never mind, about a year or two. The hon. gentleman is concerned about small matters. It is 40 years fully. This is 1905 and part of the Intercolonial Railway was running in I860. Is that not 40 years?
That is perfectly right, but I was speaking of the northern division to Moncton. +

I was speaking of the Intercolonial Railway as constituted then and making a comparison with it as constituted now. Mr. Mackenzie said that there should be an end put to the capital account on the Intercolonial Railway. Yet, we have a capital account on a road that has been running from Montreal to Halifax for 40 years for the purpose of covering up expenditures. for betterments on the road. You

will go down there and find perhaps $8,000,000 or $10,000,000 have been expended on improved facilities along the line, lengthening sidings, building sheds, and upon the smallest possible improvements and in order that the hon. gentleman may have a good showing in the House he charges these to capital account. The hon. gentleman says that these items were charged by the Conservative government in exactly be same manner. Let me tell him that when I was managing the concern such an expenditure as that at Moncton would be charged to ordinary revenue and not to capital account.
I am afraid you did not know much about it, if you make that statement.

If the hon. gentleman would have a little less of that nigger minstrel style in him and adopt a little seriousness it would add to the dignity of the proceedings and of the hon. gentleman. He has adopted that style a little too much lately and he must expect a lesson or two. He is hardly rightly seated in his position up to the present, and he is new to the proceedings of this House, but I can tell him that we have not been accustomed to that hitherto. We have been accustomed to seriousness in the debate and seriousness in answering questions, and not shifting it off in that easy, laughing, nigger minstrel style. I said that under the Conservative administration expenditures for renewing rails on the Intercolonial Railway and such like vould be charged to ordinary revenue and not to capital account. That system was changed at the instance of the late Minister of Railways, and so there can be no fair comparison made between the management of the railroad under the Conservative government and its management under the Liberal government. The only real solution of the difficulty is that proposed by my hon. friend (Mr. Osier) and that is, that it is high time that the capital account upon the Intercolonial Railway should be closed, so that the country may see at once what we are really expending on the operation of that road. It does not make much difference to those who know, how the thing is done because they can look at the expenditure on capital and the expenditure on revenue and tell at once how matters stand ; the present system only deceives the general public and it deceives them in their efforts to' make a comparison of the management of the Intercolonial Railway as between the government and the late government.

It is to be regretted I suppose that any criticism of mine should cause the hon. gentleman (Mr. Haggart) to forget the ordinary courtesy that one member owes to another. No doubt I have a great deal to learn about the proceedings of this House as well as about all other mat-Mr. HAGGART.
ters, but I believe I will have to travel further than my hon. friend to seek a competent teacher, for I fear I can learn nothing from him. The hon. gentleman made the statement that it is 40 years since the Intercolonial Railway had been completed, and that the expenditures on it have been going on since. The Intercolonial did not come into existence as such until after the year 1871, and it was not completed between Truro and Riviere du Loup until the year 1876. Before that, there were in existence two railways : one known as the European and North American running between St. John and Shediac ; the other known as the Nova Scotia Railway running from Halifax to Truro and thence to Pictou. I made the statement, and I repeat it, that since it has been an Intercolonial railway there has been a uniform rule adopted as to the charging of expenditures either to capital account on the one hand or to revenue on the other. That rule has been followed ; and it is supposed to be in accordance with the standard laid down by railway experts. There may have been variations from time to time, but that is true under every administration of the Intercolonial. I ventured to call in question the statement of my hon. friend (Mr. Haggart), that when he administered the Intercolonial, if there were new car shops or new offices constructed at Moncton, the expenditure would be charged to revenue. What seems to have made him very angry, wras my statement that he would not have given utterance to such an assertion if he were familiar with the transactions connected with the Intercolonial during his time. I speak whereof I know. I say that since it has been an Intercolonial such things as new car shops and new machinery for the construction of locomotives were charged to capital account.
Do I understand the minister to say that in my regime it was so charged 1
Yes.
I deny it.

Had I known that my hon. friend would have questioned this fact, I would have brought the proof ; the public accounts will show it clearly. But, this discussion takes place year after year and is somewhat academic, for, after all so far as the people of Canada are concerned, it is a question of bookkeeping. The bills have to be paid by the people of Canada, and whether the charge is made to capital account or to revenue account, it makes very little difference to them. Since I have been in the department, I have endeavoured to have the accounts appear as they really were. I am not afraid of deficits-
Evidently not.

X am no more afraid of deficits, incurred on the Intercolonial, than were the gentlemen on the other side of the House afraid of deficits which were incurred on the canals of Canada. I recognize the true cause of deficits on the Intercolonial, and the people who are interested in carrying out the obligations assumed at confederation also recognize that cause. We all know that the deficits on the Intercolonial are charged against the maritime provinces. But, the International is surrounded by conditions which are peculiar to that railway and to its location. I would apologize for deficits that were due to unwarranted expenditure ; I would apologize for deficits that were due to extravagance; but I am not going to apologize, I do not think there is any necessity for apologizing, for deficits that are due to causes over which I have no control, and to conditions which were connected with the Intercolonial when it was first established.

I take issue with the minister when he says that this is an academic discussion; it is a most important discussion. The accounts of the Intercolonial Railway as rendered show that the amounts charged to capital account are to a very considerable extent amounts that would not be charged to capital account by any business railway. I am not going to grumble at the cost of the Intercolonial Railway to the country. It is necessary to this country that that railway should be operated, and operated efficiently, even if it be at a loss; but it is an absolutely wrong principle to charge up that loss year after year to capital account. Let the country see and realize exactly what this railway is costing; that, is the proper and the honest way of rendering accounts. We are now face to face with a vaster problem than that of the Intercolonial Railway; we are face to face with the problem of the Transcontinental Railway fathered by this government; we are face to face with the question whether, in connection with that railway, we shall face the true position as it may turn out, or try to fool the people by adding year after year to capital account what should be charged to maintenance account. This is a most serious question for this country, because we may find ourselves in a position with respect to that road in comparison with which the deficiency in connection with the Intercolonial may be a mere bagatelle. I think it is a recognized principle that the capital expenditure on a new road during the first ten years after it is opened equals the original cost; but after a road has been running for twenty years or more, and has reached the highest standard-and the Intercolonial is at a very high standard, in my judgment, after having travelled over it last year-all charges on it should go to expenses and should not be added to the public debt of this country. There are 62
charged in this capital expenditure, amounts which no railway company, having to make a report to its shareholders, would dare to charge to capital account. I would like the minister to tell us the amount that has been expended on rolling stock, for instance and charged to capital account since 1896, also to give us a list of the rolling stock as it now exists, with a statement of its value; and I think we shall find that millions of dollars properly chargeable to revenue account, have been charged to capital account. I do not think the minister can point to a single railway report in the library which shows the same class of items as are contained in this list charged to capital account. This is a good time to bring this matter up, so that we may know bow these charges are going to be made in connection with the Transcontinental Railway.'

We have come to a point in reference to the Intercolonial Railway and its management which I think is somewhat of a crisis; and, so far as I am concerned, I propose to push the question until we get down to some settled system of making a balance sheet which will show the general results of the operation of that road.
I take exception to one remark of the hon. minister, and I do it with all kindness to him. He says that it makes no difference whether you charge the expenditure on the road to capital account or to running expenses, that it is a mere matter of bookkeeping, and that in either the country has to pay. I take strong exception to that. It makes no difference, may be, so far as the total amount of money to be paid by the country in a single year is concerned; but it makes very great differences in other respects. If you are going to charge these expenditures to capital account just as it pleases you for the time being, and that becomes the practice, it tends inevitably to extravagance in the management of the road. The minister may be the best possible kind of a minister ; but so long as he can dip into the public till for expenditures of different kinds, with the tremendous pressure which is behind him-and no one knows that better than the minister himself-he will be met by regular appeal, what does it matter to you?. Just charge that to capital expenditure, and it does not appear in the deficit.
I say it has a most injurious effect, and it tends to extravagance which will increase from year to year. It has another effect.
It not only tends to extravagance so far as the administration of the department by the minister is concerned, but it puts jtlie whole business in a false light before the country, and tends to prevent the country from being aroused to the real facts of the case, and to the necessity of making its protest and its pressure for improvement. The country is not so apt to take into con-



sideration the capital expenditure upon a road as the difference between the running expenses and the current income. If, therefore, by this easy method, which is nothing more than bookkeeping, you can charge to capital that ought to go into current expenditure, and which would therefore swell the deficit, you prevent the people from knowing the real state of things and consequently prevent the remedy from being applied. Now, the Prime Minister, not once, but many times in the province of Ontario, if not elsewhere, made this statement in the course of the last election, that the Intercolonial Bailway was an instance which would serve as a compleate warning to any government undertaking to operate a road under government ownership. He said that it never had paid, that no minister had been able to make it pay, which was rot quite correct, so far as meeting the ordinary yearly expenses by the receipts was concerned. Of course, if you take interest into account, no minister ever made it pay.
He bethought himself just then that he would make a condemnation of his own ministers in that respect, and he gave the reason why ; he said it was because it was managed under a vicious system. That was a very strong statement for the Prime Minister of a country to make, that an immense road, the operation of which involved millions of dollars of current expenditures and capital expenditures, was an unproductive road, and was in a state of constant and chronic deficit, because, forsooth, it was managed under a vicious system. The country has come to the point, I think, that it wishes to inquire into that system, and to see whether there is not a better one. It will certainly not be helped in that inquiry by a loose system of charging to capital expenditure what ought to go to current account, even although it would swell the deficit. There is another remark to which I wish to take exception. I notice that the minister of late has taken it into his head to make a ready answer to all allegations of large expenses and inadequate returns, as compared with other roads, by saying that it was never intended that the Intercolonial Railway should pay, that it was a road conceived under conditions which were not considered absolutely essential to a paying road; that it is a convenience for transportation and connection between outlying and distant provinces, and consequently is not to be treated as a commercial road. There is something in that argument, but it can be made too much of, and I think the minister is 'making too much of it in using it every time as a mitigation of large deficits and expenses. It is true there were deficits, but it is also true that it was never contemplated. and never need be contemplated, that the Intercolonial Railway, if well managed, would not be able to pay its current expenses and. at the same time, be run as an up-to-date railway. I have no doubt that Mr. FOSTER.
the Intercolonial Railway, if it were run under a proper and not under a vicious system, would be able to pay its expenses from year to year, and conduct its business on the same lines as other great railways do with regard to capital and current expenditures. In one of the best years in a series of the best years Canada has had, during which all other railways are showing increased traffic and decreased expenses or, if not both of these, increased net profits year by year, here we have at the end of these prosperous years the Intercolonial Railway, which has been in operation for thirty years, with a settled road and a fine roadbed, with all its initial expenses paid, showing a larger deficit than it has ever had before. These are things that need to be taken up seriously by both sides. I am not finding fault with the officials of the railways; I believe that one of the good characteristics of the management of the road by my hon. friend from Lanark (Mr. Haggart) was that he largely threw the responsibility of management on the officers of the road, that he largely gave to them the power of employing as many men as they wished and no more than they wished, and of dismissing men who were inefficient. How is it to-day ? We find the vicious system that the Prime Minister spoke of, this miserable system of patronage which, from the furthest end of the Intercolonial Railway until you get up to Montreal, is the bane and curse of that railway. I say that there is not a shadow of doubt in my mind, that if you were to put the management of that railway in the hands of a commission of men who were free from the annoyance and expense of partisan appointments, and were held responsible for the management of that road, the Intercolonial Railway could be made to pay. It cannot be made to pay under the present arrangement, under which, from end to end of the road, there is a constant fight carried on by outsiders to shove men into the service, and few ministers are strong enough to stand up against that pressure. These are matters to which I wish to call the minister's attention. They will be discussed in this House, and the country is in the mood for seeing them discussed and settled. I hope we will take hold of this subject, not so much by one making charges and another defending himself against the charges, but by sitting down together on both sides of the House trying if we cannot make the Intercolonial Railway a better road than it is, not so much in equipment of rolling stock and perfection of roadbed, as in the methods of management and the returns it makes to the country.

I have in the last three or four sessions discussed the questions that have now been discussed by the hon. member for South Lanark (Mr. Haggart), the member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) and the member for West Toronto (Mr. Osier) ;

and I do not think that the long discussions we have had upon this subject of capital account were wholly without effect even upon the government. The hon. gentleman has told us this year that his loss in working the Intercolonial Railway was something near $1,000,000. That was dead loss to the country in the operation of the road at a time when all the other companies are working with very handsome profits. What I have contended year after year since I have had the honour of being in this House was that the government were so keeping the accounts of this government railway that it was absolutely impossible to compare the management under this government with the management of previous governments, and that it was even impossible to compare the management in one year under the present government with the management in another year. There ought not to be any difference whatever between the system of keeping the accounts of this government railway and the accounts of ordinary railway companies. If anything, the government should be more determined even than other companies to abolish, if possible, the capital account. Instead of the government doing that, it has been their policy year after year to avoid the fair responsibility for working expenses,; and to make fictitious profits or reduce the actual losses of operation by what would be called hocussing the accounts if the same things were done by an ordinary corporation. I have on many occasions in this House had to call attention to the manner in which the rolling stock was maintained, and I am glad to say that during the past year the hon. gentleman who now is at the head of the department has done something to improve matters in that respect. I think that the account he has brought down, bad as it is, far as it is from being what it ought to be, is far better than, as regards rolling stock, it has been during the last five years. He has got back near to what the maintenance of rolling stock was under the administration of the hon. member for South Lanark (Mr. Haggart). But the hon. gentleman has charged up to capital account, that is he has added to the debt of this country, the cost of 235 articles of rolling stock, from locomotives down to flat cars.
Now, while the hon. gentleman has done that, he has actually had dead stock that he ought to have repaired and put into service,, charging the expenditure to working expenses, to a greater number than he bought at the cost of the country. At the end of the year he had 268 articles of rolling stock absolutely out of service, unfit for any use and not capable of rep'air, according to his own statement. With this number of all descriptions out of service, he buys an extra 235 and charges them up to the debt of the country. Now, what possible excuse can there be for anything of that kind ?
The hon. gentleman may say, perhaps, that a few of them would fall into decay or be broken up in the last few months of the year. But 119 of these were actually out during the whole year, and returned by him the previous year as being unserviceable and requiring to be rebuilt. He shows that on the face of his report. He starts with 585 out of service at the beginning of the year. He rebuilds 466, and the difference 119, he carries as dead stock, old lumber, for the whole twelve months not spending one dollar upon them. He is enabled to do that of course, because he has a splendid paymaster behind him, and charges the new stock to the debt of the country. What could exemplify more clearly the danger and folly of carrying out this system ? It has been pointed out over and over again, and shown by the figures from the minister's report, that the predecessor of the hon. gentleman when, in certain years, he showed a small profit in the working of the railway, had he kept his accounts according to the ordinary system of companies, instead of a profit would have had a very large deficit. Yet, in the face of that fact, we had the Finance Minister telling the House and the country how gratifying it was to find that under the administration of this government the Intercolonial line, which had formerly been worked at a loss, was now a source of profit to the country. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Emmerson) is reaping some of the results of that course. He has had to go into the repairing of rolling stock. If these 585 articles of the rolling stock had been kept up as an ordinary railway company would have kept them up, the hon. gentleman would have been saved a large expenditure. But he has had to do this year more than his predecessor had to do in the same time. His predecessor would have made a very vigorous effort to show a profit instead of this loss of over a million dollars. And the hon. gentleman (Mr. Emmerson) himself has not had the backbone to face the situation, but has carried over 268 articles of rolling stock and replaced them with 235 at the expense of the country. I do not wish to spend time on this subject. The matter has been fully dealt with. All I say Is that on a government kailway every effort should be made-and I do not see any difficulty in carrying it out-to absolutely abolish the capital account. It has been laid down by many writers on railway subjects that the true principle is this :	Once a railway
undertaking is in operation, it should maintain itself, and, according as it succeeds or fails in doing that it is to be judged as a prof table or losing concern. It may be very difficult to carry that out in the case of a private corporation that has to borrow money from the banks and from the public and must sometimes yield to necessity. But there is no reason whatever why a great country like the Dominion of Canada should have to make any pretense in these matters.

If our great railway is failing to carry itself, why should not that fact be made known to the' public ? It may be said that in the east they do not desire to have a bad showing for the road at the end of the year. I think that is a mistake. 1 think, that, in the interest of the maritime provinces the actual working operations and conditions of the road should be shown. No person in the western provinces desires to interfere for a moment with the operation of the Intercolonial line. No one wants to look upon it as a drag upon the country. We recognize its usefulness ; we know what its object was, and we are prepared to stand by it. But, in the interest of the country, in the interest of the maritime provinces themselves, whose people, I am sure,' are just as anxious to see the accounts properly kept as we are, a change should be made. Therefore, I never had any hesitation, any more than I have at this moment, in criticising fairly what I think is wrong on the part of the government in the management of this road. And, with regard to this matter of rolling stock and other items that will come up presently, I say, unless the hon. gentleman (Mr. Emmerson) makes a reform in the keeping of the accounts we shall never know, during the existence of this government, what that road is earning or losing.

I gladly add my opinion to those that have been expressed by hon. gentlemen within the last hour or so as to the mode of keeping the accounts of the Intercolonial line. I have never hesitated in this House, in years gone by, to declare that I thought the time had arrived, even with the public accounts of the Dominion of Canada, that there should be no capital account. There can be no question about it that throughout the country many people are misled as to the actual results of the financial operations of any particular year. Last year, we were told that we had a surplus of some sixteen and a half millions of dollars ; and, doubtless, many people in the country believed that such a surplus actually existed. But the public accounts tell a very different story, when we put the two accounts together and compare our total revenue and our total expenditure. I hold that it is not treating the public fairly to keep the accounts any longer in this way, because there is doubtless a very great misapprehension in the mind of the general public. Now. if that applies to the Dominion of Canada, it applies with at least equal force to the Intercolonial Railway. There are many people who believe that in bygone years, more particularly under the regime of the present government, the Intercolonial was a paying institution, notwithstanding the fact that during the first five years of the present government that road actually cost the country some $13,000,000 more than the revenue derived from it.
I say that condition of things ought not to exist. It is the people's road, and the people ought to know without any doubt what it costs to operate the road. I heartily approve the sentiments expressed here today, that some change ought to be made in the system of keeping the accounts of this road. At any rate, the public should be made aware at the end of every financial year exactly how much the road has cost, all told, more than the revenue derived from it. I am not one of those who want the Intercolonial to be a money-making institution for the country, I do not consider that is the purpose of public works. We do not expect to get profit from our canals, we do not expect to get profit out of the expenditure we make on the St. Lawrence river and other rivers, or out of the many harbours that we dredge and spend public money on-we do not expect to get a direct profit ; the profit comes in an indirect way, and the same with the Intercolonial. It is the people's road, it is there for a purpose, and as long as it accomplishes that purpose without a loss to the country. I think the country will be satisfied. But the country will not be satisfied to find out in after years that we are loaded up with many millions of addition to our public debt on account of the operations on this road, when from time to time and from year to year they were given to understand that a surplus had been earned by the road. I trust the minister will give consideration to this question. I will hail with delight the time when a change will be made in the whole system, and when the people of this country who own that road shall know each year what the road is costing over and above the earnings. In no other way do I believe that the expenditure will be brought within the revenue. I think a change of system in the book-keeping on that road would be the first means of drawing attention to it and bringing the cost of maintenance within the scope of the revenue derived from the earnings of the road.
Drummondville-improvements at, $23,000.
What are the improvements at Drummondville ?
A new station, a platform, the purchase of land, and converting the present station into a freight shed. It is also required to put in a tank there, and we want additional sidings.
Now would the minister in this case, as a sample of what he ought to do in every case, read the details of the estimate, how much for each thing that is going to be done ?
Station and platform, $12,500 ; land, $2,000 ; extension and making new engine-house to meet additional sized engines, $1,500 ; freight shed, $1,500; building a tank, $5,500; electric wiring,
l$500 ; additional sidings and cost of engineering, $4,500, making in all $28,000. We estimate the expenditure made this year at $5,000.
What is the cost of engineering ?
The whole cost of engineering, with advertising and inspecting, $1,500, leaving a balance of $23,000, $11,000 of which is a revote.
What have you there now ?
We have an old station that we have to abandon, but it will be used as a freight shed. We have to build a new station and acquire land for it.
Surely charging a new tank to capital is going too far.
It is not replacing one.

speechtext:
The hon. gentleman means a charge instead of a credit. So much depreciation of property should be charged up against the profits.
iMr. TAYLOR. It is credited to the machinery account. The machinery account is reduced in value ten per cent every year and charged to profit and loss.
The result is the same.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: But the hon. minister does not take the expenditure out of current revenue, but charges it to capital as he has done at Drummondville in connection with the building of a new platform when there is already a good platform there. I notice in the estimates an item for new machinery for locomotive and car shops. This is the ordinary machinery required to repair something that has gone out of order, yet, it is charged to capital account.
I can explain that to my hon. friend.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
In addition, I find semaphores charged to capital account and the replacing of a building which has been worn out in the service is also charged to capital account. There surely ought to be something taken out of current expenditure to replace a building and to replace ordinary rolling stock. This is a matter to which my hon. friend from Hamilton (Mr. Barker) referred a short time ago. A lot of new cars were bought to replace old ones which had been worn out in the service and they were

charged to capital account. I do not think it is in accordance with business principles to allow expenditures that ought to be chargeable to ordinary expenditure to be charged to capital account. These expenditures should be charged to capital account bo as to let the people know at once how much this road is losing for them. If that were done the people of this country would soon say : Let us try running this road without a political head. Let us put it in the hands of a commission and run it on business principles. I do not know that the tariff of rates should be as high as those on other railways, although it is pretty high. I am a large shipper over that road down through that eastern country, and I find they charge good rates going down, whatever they may be coming up. Let the rates be fixed at a price to pay running expenses if they do not pay interest, but certainly the accounts, should be kept in a different manner.
In this case where you make a freight shed out of an old station do you charge the making of the change to capital account ?
Yes, because the other building is still in existence as part of a capital investment and this is a new station, something that they have not had before. They have not had facilities there.
But, you have a station there now and you are going to build a new station.
It is a freight shed now. There has been no such thing previously.
You called it a station.
It was a so called.
Well, you are going to make some little changes in the station and call it a freight shed.
No, it is absolutely a new station.
I am not talking of the station. I am talking of the freight shed.
It is to be converted into a freight shed.
You say it is a freight shed now.
No, it is a building that has been utilized as a station. We are going to utilize it as a freight shed.
How much work are you going to do on it ?
There is very little work to be done on it.
And yet you charge that to capital ?
