speechtext: Do they charge a door knob to capital ?

Do they charge a door knob to capital ? Yes. Why, they charge for renewing a portion of a partition simply in some of the offices in Moncton. I am making a list. I will have a very interesting list when we take up this discussion again. Items of $7.50, $4 and $5 for little things that are necessary improvements are all zealously charged to capital account, small in themselves, but in the whole going up to tens of thousands of dollars.

The machinery referred to by my hon. friend from Leeds (Mr. Taylor) is machinery that is required for the construction of engines. A session or two ago the hon. gentleman who was then the member for Jacques Cartier and who to-day represents that constituency (Mr. Monk) pointed out, that it would be in the interest of economy on the Intercolonial Railway that locomotives should be constructed, and he advised, and at that time the committee advised, that the work should be extended so that they could with facility and under economical conditions construct locomotives. In accordance with that idea a new erecting shop is about being constructed and new machinery to equip it is being furnished. This vote includes these provisions.

Here is another sample I have just got hold of. There was a baggage-room somewhere. It had been in use, I do not know how long, but it came to be necessary to remove that baggage-room a little way and they charged that moving, costing a few dollars, to capital account.
Where was that ?
I will find out where that was.

I would like to ask the hon. minister to give the committee the benefit of his experience in respect to the manufacture of locomotives and cars under the management of the Intercolonial Railway as compared with those that have been purchased elsewhere.

The year before last three or four locomotives were turned out from the workshops at Moncton. I have understood, and I make this statement on the authority of the practical men who run these locomotives, the locomotive engineers themselves, that they are really a class of locomotives superior to any that have been purchased either in Canada or out of it. That may be a natural prejudice on the part of the men in favour of the products of the Intercolonial workshops, but it is the testimony-given for what it is worth-of the employees of the road who are locomotive engineers. I have heard machinists say the same thing and these locomotives

are of a very superior class as I believe. They are very durable. They have a number of locomotives on the Intercolonial Railway that have seen pretty hard service, that have been in use for years and they are said to have proved the durability of the work that has been done there. They do not make any new cars as far as I am aware. They reconstruct them and in this connection I will deal with the question raised by my hon. friend for Hamilton (Mr. Barker)'and' I will be able to place him in possession of more information in connection with these operations. But, I think I can fairly say that during the past year there has been more of that reconstruction work in the workshops at Moncton and elsewhere on the Intercolonial Railway than has ever before been the case, and that increased efforts are being made in that direction.
I said so in regard to the last four or five years.
'When another item is reached I will be able to furnish my hon. friend with additional data to confirm him in his judgment.
To what account are the wages charged when you replace light rails with heavier rails.
I am told they are charged to revenue.
Were these four locomotives constructed at Moncton, built as cheaply as locomotives of the same kind and capacity could be purchased outside ?

Until the past couple of years I do not think there was a strict account kept of the cost of each particular locomotive. Under the present administration of the mechanical department, I understand that such is being done. There have been no locomotives constructed during the past year, so that we have no record to go by. I have been informed by the superintendent of motive power, that engines can be built at Moncton as cheaply as they can be purchased elsewhere. Of course I am speaking generally, and I do not say that that takes into account interest on the expenditure for shops and machinery. My statement is simply from a conversation which took place on this very point, and I would not wish to be bound to exact data in that respect.
What is the capacity of these shops ?

I have explained that ell the parts were not constructed at Moncton because we did not have the necessary machinery. Certain parts of the locomotives were purchased and brought to Moncton, but it is now proposed to get machinery to enable us to construct practically everything that goes into a locomotive.
How many engines a year will you turn out ?
We probably cannot turn out very many, but this machinery will enable us to begin.

To expend money for the purpose of erecting shops with the idea of experimenting on turning out four or five engines a year is an absolute waste of money.
Mr, EMMERSON. That is the abstract truth, but I may say that we have large shops at Moncton, and while we are not going into the business of constructing locomotives, yet we intend to have machinery which wiil enable us to do all kinds of repairing. Incidentally, when the men are not engaged in repairing work their time can be devoted to the construction of new lccomotives. I do not think it mould pay to put up a shop for the construction of locomotives, especially when these shops would only have a limited capacity, but I do believe it would pay to do. all our repairing and incidentally to construct locomotives.
It will not pay to build them in any shape or way.

This expenditure is not in the interests of the people. It ought to be the policy of the government to establish a complete repair shop, manned to meet the requirements of the road, but to speak of purchasing machinery to enable men not otherwise engaged to produce new locomotives is a thing that no successful business man would think of. When the minister asked for this vote of $92,000 he surely must have had some carefully considered plan, and he should be able to tell us what results can be obtained from such an expenditure. Is it the intention of the government to commence the manufacturing of locomotives.

I thought I made myself understood. It is not necessary for us to commence the building of locomotives. We have been building them, and it is proposed to continue, and incidentally to utilize the machinery which is absolutely necessary for the economical repairing of engines.
With regard to the four locomotives which the minister said he had constructed, were they constructed on revenue account or on capital account ?
They were constructed on revenue account.
Then I presume the hon. gentleman is not able to give us the exact cost of these ?
Oh, no.

And there are no means by which we can ascertain whether the locomotives are being expensively built as

compared with the cost of purchasing or not ?

No, only a general statement.
Intercolonial Railway-increased accommodation at Antigonish, $9,000.

This is a revote. Last session $14,000 was voted for a new station. The total cost of the work will be $14,000.
Intercolonial Railway-improvements at Newcastle. $25,500.
This is a new vote, and we want a full explanation of it.
This is for an enlargement of the engine house to meet the necessities in conn x-t'ou with the new locomotives,
How many additional stalls ?
There are eighteen stalls. This does not increase their number, but it lengthens them to enable us to accommodate the new and enlarged engines.
How much does the hon. gentleman propose to use in enlarging the engine house ?
$20,000. We propose also to put in a water service at a cost of $4,000, and the cost of engineering inspection is $1,500, making a total of $25,500.
Are these charges in connection with your own men on the railway ?
We have engineers employed in connection with capital expenditure.
Will this be let by contract ?
Yes.
What is the cost of the engineering ?
It is not given separately in the details furnished topne, hut I am told that it is between $400 and $500.
On almost every item which has been under discussion this afternoon, there is a considerable charge for engineering. I would like to know what engineers these are ?

We have on the Intercolonial Railway what are called construction engineers. They are not connected with the maintenance of way engineering department ; but construction work required anywhere on the line or on the Prince Edward Island Railway is done under their supervision, and the time expended by them in connection with each work is chargeable to that work.
Mr. OSLER How many such engineers have you employed, are they on the perma-Mr. BARKER.
nent list, and if so will you give us their names ?
Including the draughtsmen there are about ten.
If there are ten on new construction work, I think we are entitled to know their names and the salaries paid to them.
And where they are stationed.
The headquarters of all of them are at Moncton.
We would like to know what their pay is and under whose supervision they are.

They are under the supervision of Mr. W. B. Mackenzie, the chief engineer, and comprise his staff. Some of them are draughting engineers, others are those who go out and supervise construction, make surveys and examinations. They are really a permanent staff. Their salary is apportioned and charged up against each particular work in proportion to the amount of time these officers spend on it. That system has been in vogue for a long time.
They are appointed by the chief engineer ?

I think most of them have been there for years. I do not know who made the appointments, I know that I have made none ; the staff was there when I went into the department. The members of the staff are :

Then each year about $15,500 of salary is charged to capital account ?
Yes.
They are all charged to capital account whether there is any work done or not ?

I can assure my hon. friend that they are all at work. I personally know that.
Campbellton-improvements at, $12,000.
That is a new vote.

Yes, that is a new item. We are putting in there an ash conveyor, to cost $1,000 ; a sand drying apparatus and building, at a cost of $2,000 ; an extension of the water supply to cost $3,000, and we are putting up a building

for express and baggage and conductors that will cost $3,000 ; a freight shed, $1,500, and a building for car inspector to cost $300. Here comes in again the engineering item of $1,200, making a total of $12,000.
It appears to me that the total of the amounts voted in this way for engineering in the different items come to more than the $15,500 for salaries.

It is not all for engineers ; it includes the inspection work. There has to be an inspector on all these works employed by the day. The specifications are prepared, the plans are all made and it is advertised ; the contract is entered into, and the inspector employed and is paid per diem.
Is he a regular officer of the department ?
No, generally we employ some skilled man, usually in the community.
As a rule, it is somebody who has had experience in that line. He may be a friend of the contractor if he is a local man.
We generally succeed in avoiding that.
The man who gets the contract is generally a friend of the government, and I presume the inspector is too.
As a rule, the local men do not get the contract. I do not know how it is, but not in one case in fifty does a local man get the contract.
Why does the hon. minister employ inspectors for this work when he has his own staff of engineers ?
We want a man there by the day.
But the minister has his own staff. Why, then, should he employ an outsider ?

Because it is absolutely necessary. You would not want to have an engineer from Moncton on each of these works and staying on the work from early morning until night. We want a man who is a practical, skilled man, a man with knowledge of the actual work. He stands over the contractor and sees to it that the specifications are carried out.
Pretty expensive men.

I think it pays.
Intercolonial Railway-diversion of public road to eliminate a crossing at rail-level between St. Cyrille and Drummondville, $500.
How about this crossing?

That is a re-vote. The work is done under arrangements entered
into with the municipality to change the roadway. It is a saving to the railway.
Does the municipality pay part?

Yes.
Intercolonial Railway-additional sidings and spur lines, $135,800.
I think we must ask the minister to give us detailed information about this, and I doubt whether he would be able to do it now.

I can hardly do it before six o'clock.
At six o'clock, committee took recess.
After Recess.
Committee resumed at eight o'clock.
Intercolonial Railway-additional sidings and spur lines, $135,800,

1 would ask the minister, with regard to this item and all similar items, to give us as minute details as possible. We want-to know where the sidings are to be constructed, and we want to know it, I may tell the minister, for this purpose : Eighteen months or two years hence we will be discussing the expenditures now authorized, and whoever will occupy our seats at that time will want to be able to refer to what the minister says to-day of the purposes for which he asks this money. I would like him, therefore, to tell us what sidings he proposes to construct, where they are, and the amount for each.

Hon. members will see that last year we had a vote of $23,700 for spur lines, aside from the sidings. Now this year we have combined the two. There is required for a spur line from Port Lawrence, in Cumberland county, to the government wharf, estimated to cost $15,000, it is 1'23 miles in length. We will require a spur line west of Riviere Ouelle which is estimated to cost $8,000, and is 1:45 miles long. We will require a spur liue at Trois Pistoles, estimated to cost $10,500, length 2i miles. We will require an extension of sidings at Jefferson's, to cost $1,000.
What is the length ?
We have not got the length, it is an extension.
That is just one of the particulars we desire. You have a siding there now, we want to know how much you are going to add to it.
We want to extend that siding in order to accommodate the longer trains we are now hauling over the Intercolonial.
How many feet ?
I have not here the length of these sidings.

I would point out to the minister that before he authorized the application for this $1,000 to His Excellency the Governor in Council, tne minister must have satisfied himself from the officials of his department that it was required. Now we uant to know that, because we have been going on year after year authorizing millions of money for this road, and we have come to the conclusion it is about time a little effort were made, on the part of the opposition at all events, to know just what the money is wanted for.

I am endeavouring to give that information. It is a mere matter of the extension of a siding. On the advice of the engineers, I authorized it to be put in the estimates, relying upon the accuracy of their judgment and their bona fides as to the estimated cost. It could uot be expected of me that I would be able to judge personally as to whether their figures were correct, even though an exact limit were given. I hardly think it would be expected of me to figure out and compute in all circumstances, the exact cost. They make their report, and they say a certain amount of money is required for an extension of a siding. They state that the siding at Jefferson's will cost $1,000.

Will the minister allow me to interrupt him ? What we object to, and what we have been continually objecting to for three or four years, is that the minister of the department-I am not finding fault only with the present minister-has asked for $150,000 or $135,000, as the case may be, for a lot of sidings. He may spend $500 on one siding, on this one for instance, instead of $1,000 and then, if he pleases, he may spend the other $500 on some other siding that he has not been authorized to spend it upon. We want to know exactly what is wanted for these sidings, how many feet the extension of each is and all about them.

As far as the money -that is appropriated now is concerned, the money in each particular item is applied to that item. It is not diverted. We discussed this matter last year, the items were gone over in detail and I have required this year a specific statement as to the cost of each particular extension of a siding. I have not asked particularly for the information as to the length. I suppose I might have done that. But, each particular item asked for, the details of which I am endeavouring to give, is for the particular work named and is to be applied to that particular work.

I think we are entitled to know the length, but I do not wish to delay matters. I understand the hon. min-Mr. BARKER.
ister now to say to us that this vote of $1,000 is appropriated specifically to Jefferson's siding, and that if it is not used for that purpose it will not be used for any other purpose.
No, it will not be.

So that the Auditor General will be governed accordingly. The hon. minister will recollect the reason why I make the point. Two or three years ago money granted in 'bulk was taken by the minister of the day and used for purposes quite outside of the vote. The Auditor General then said that he thought it was wrong, but if the hon. minister puts himself on record now that this $1,000, if not used for this purpose, shall not be used for any other purpose, I am content.

Certainly, we discussed the matter and I remember my hon. friend taking the same ground last year that he takes now. I was quite in accord with' him and at that time in the supplementary estimates there were more particulars given in reference to these sidings than had been given in the main estimates. I had nothing to do with the preparation of the main estimates last year, but this year in preparing the main estimates particular amounts were assigned to the particular works for which they are asked and they will be so applied. At Monastery, there is to be an extension of the loading siding which is estimated to cost $300. At South River a loading siding is estimated to cost $800. Between New Glasgow and Wood-burn there is a crossing siding required that will cost $3,500. At Pictou Landing, opposite the town of Pictou, there is a siding in connection with the shipments of coal which will cost $4,000.
Why should that not be a specific grant ?

Well, with the view of not multiplying the number of resolutions in the estimates, I have grouped these together in such a way that there will not be such a mass of detail or such a number of specific items as there otherwise would be.

That is another point, if the hon. minister will allow me, that we called attention to last year. The hon. gentleman, for instance, in these preliminary estimates-I presume they are only a small part of what we will ultimately have before us-is asking for $2,676,000 in about three quarters of a page. The saving of a page or two of printing may be very important to the hon. minister, but it strikes me that if a little more expenditure was devoted to printing, say, about two pages more in these estimates, thus giving us such a detail as $4,000 for the siding at Pictou, it would be somewhat to the public advantage. I call

the bon. gentleman's attention to. bis own estimates in tbe canal department, because tbe bon. gentleman there does not object to giving us an item of $500, or $000. He takes up three or four pages with those estimates.
Mr. EMMERSOX'. I have in these given an item of $500.

I know, but here are tbe whole estimates amounting to $2,676,000 given in about three quarters of a page. He cannot help what is past, but I appeal to the hon. gentleman that this point will not be overlooked in the preparation of the supplementary estimates. He knows exactly what I am driving at. He knows what has been said year after year here, and I ask him to be a little more specific in these things. It does not add any appreciable amount to the expense of printing. The cost of printing is nothing to the cost of the time that we spend in discussing the matter here and which would be saved if he would give us some details in these estimates.

I had in view the idea of saving a little of the time of the committee in preparing the estimates in this way. I see what my hon. friend contends for. Then, there is the Glengarry loading siding w7hich is estimated to cost $500. At Windsor Junction we want additional sidings and these will cost $10,500. Windsor Junction is the point where the Dominion Atlantic connects with the Windsor Branch Railway which is part of the Intercolonial Railway system and also connects with the Midland Railway which runs through the counties of Hants and Colchester to Truro.

Will the hon. minister allow me to use that illustration to show what I mean ? He is asking for a vote of $135,800 of which he proposes to spend $10,500 for sidings at Windsor Junction. Gentleman from New Brunswick or Nova Scotia taking up these Intercolonial estimates and seeing that item of $135,800 cannot give any of us the slightest information, but if they were so set out as to show these items of $10,500 for sidings at Windsor Junction, $4 000 for a siding at Pictou and $500 for the Glengarry loading siding, these gentlemen would tell us at once that these were all right or the opposite as the case might be. I think some hon. gentleman told us last year that it cost us $28 a minute to carry on the proceedings of the House. We lose five minutes discussing a question of $500 when, if these estimates were printed in a little more detail, all these items might pass without observation.
I think I would be willing Jo make almost any sacrifice of principle in order to save the time of the committee.

I would like to say that the hon. minister has given us a number of sidings that he is asking $59,500 to construct. He has $19,700 more than he wants, but he does not tell us how many sidings he proposes to construct with that money. The engineer, and in some cases the road-master, is sent out to make a report on the extent of the siding needed and its probable cost, and the railway authorities must have that information. Unless the House gets it we cannot know what the minister is doing with the money. We should know how many feet will be built each year, or else it would be quite possible to take this money and devote it to some other purpose.

I will give the details. At Enfield, extension of siding, $200 ; Oxford junction, additional siding and loading ground, $7,000 ; Springhill junction, additional siding, $7,000 ; Aulac, loading siding, $1,000 ; Bloomfield, extending crossing siding, $1,500 ; Penobsquis, extending crossing siding, $4,000 ; Catamount, extension of siding, $200 ; O'Brien's crossing, three miles west of Beaver Brook, siding, $500 ; at a point two miles west of Bartibogue, siding, $500 ; at Bentpoint, crossing, siding, $4,000 ; at Beresford, extension of loading siding, $4,900 ; Dalhousie junction, extension of siding, $700 ; Elat Bands, crossing siding, $4,000 ; Causapscal, extension of siding and crossing siding, $4,400 Amqui, loading siding, $500 ; Cedar Hall extension of siding, $600 ; top of grade west of St. Moise, siding, $2,700 ; at Kempt, loading siding, $1,250 ; Rimouski wharf, branch siding. $500 ; Sacre Cceur, extension of siding, $1,500 ; top of the grade west of Bic, crossing siding, $3,000 ; St. Fabien, extension crossing siding, $2,000 ; -St. Cimon, extension of loading siding, $750 ; St. Arsene, extension crossing siding, $500 ; Riviere du Boup wharf, branch siding, $4,000 ; Old Bake road, crossing siding, $4,000 ; St. Andre, extension of crossing siding, $1,200 j Ste'. Bouise, extension of crossing siding, $1,250 ; Elgin road, extension crossing siding, $500 ; St. Jean, Port Joli, $1,200 ; Trois Saumons, $600 ; B'lslet, siding, $3,500 ; Cap St. Ignac, construction of a ' Y,' $2,500 ; St. Francois, extension of crossing siding and loading siding, $1,500 ; St. Henri junction, crossing siding, $3,500 ; siding for transferring cars from Intercolonial Railway to Quebec Central Railway, $500 ; St. Jean Chrysostfime, extension of loading siding and filling for loading ground, $1,500 ; Chaudiere, curve siding, $500 ; St. Nicolas, siding, $500 ; Ni-colet, siding, $1,100; Carmel, to extend loading siding, $1,500 ; contingencies covering items of engineering, &c., $7,950.

The hon. gentleman has about forty-five items running from $500 to $18,000, and I am quite sure that he will see that there is very little use in the opposition criticising these estimates unless the gentlemen who represent the districts affected

liave an opportunity of knowing what the proposed expenditures are. If we had in the estimates these particulars which the hon. gentleman has read in about fifteen minutes, they could have been given in about a quarter of a page. We would then have had the information in regard to every one of these items, and we would have known whether they were proper items from our point of view, or whether there was anything to criticise in them. As it is, we come here and have about one minute's consideration to give to each item. We cannot do our duty in criticising the estimates, and we may occupy time which is valuable and costly. The hon. gentleman will expend in a discussion of this kind more money than would build one of these short sidings.

It is unfair to expect this side of the House to approve of this vote with the limited amount of information which is given us. The minister might as well offer no information to the House at all. Every year similar votes are asked for. I think the parties who have recommended the construction of these sidings should have stated the number of feet to be constructed, and the supposed cost. If we had that information, the report of the minister of the following year would tell us exactly what had been done. Otherwise, we are in the dark, and the hon. minister might as well expect these items to go through without ottering any information. I for one protest against it.
The items are purely departmental, recommended by the engineer and the management of the Intercolonial, and I thought I would save the time of the committee by having them grouped together.

I think I can figure out exactly how these items have come to be placed in the hon. gentleman's estimates. Supporters of the government through whose constituencies this railway runs, go to the department and say, it Is necessary, in order to meet the requirements of this particular district, that the sidings should be extended. The railway officials in the department ask : What will it cost ? The answer is that it will cost $1,000, $2,000, $3,000, or $4,000, as the case may be. The item is recommended to Council, and it appears in the hon. gentleman's estimates, and when he is asked for the information in this House, he is not able to give it, because I venture to say that his officers have not figured out the number of feet or the estimated cost of the siding. That is the way it occurs to me that these items have been placed in the hon. gentleman's estimates ; because if the engineer asked for any of these sidings, he would state the number of feet and give the estimated cost in a businesslike way. In one instance, where $59,000 is to be expended, the hon. gentleman Mr. BARKER.
has told us the number of feet; but in another case where he is going to spend double that amount, he cannot tell us the number of feet. There is not a railway company in America that would make a proposition of that kind to its directors without giving the particulars.

My hon. friend has drawn on his imagination. I do not know what weight any assurance I could give to my hon. friend would have, but I can only say to him, and I say it with a full knowledge of all that my words import, that there is not a single item of all these sidings mentioned here that has been the subject matter of any representative of a constituency going to the officials and making representations in the way my hon. friend has described. More than that, there is not a single siding that has not been surveyed and been the subject matter of inquiry by the officials themselves ; and I have no doubt that all these details as to the length of each siding are in the possession of the engineers. I have said very frankly that I have not that, that I had not asked for it ; because, relying upon the reports of the engineers that a certain siding was required and that it would cost so much, I authorized the vote for it to be placed in the estimates. I am quite sure that was the case with all these items.
Will the hon. minister be able to give us the lengths of these various sidings if we allow the item to stand until to-morrow ?

I would have.to send to Moncton for that. I will furnish that information afterwards in connection with j some supplementary estimates, so that it can be placed in 'Hansard.'
Intercolonial Railway-station at St. Moise, $2,300.
When there are several items for the one place, as at St. Moise. they should be all placed together.
This work is west of St. Moi'se station.
How large a place is this?
St. Moi'se is a summer resort on the lower St. Lawrence, a growing place.
What is the population?

I do not know the exact population, but I know that this station serves a very large back country. It is not simply the cluster of houses around the station that is to be considered, but the amount of traffic that is assembled there from the surrounding districts.
I think this is another case in which the minister is drawing on his imagination.
I am familiar with the place; I have been there.

A freight shed was moved and extended there last year on which yon spent 81,500; now you propose to spend $2,300. That is $5,800 at this very important place as the minister says, drawing on his imagination.

I am open to all kinds of charges, but I do not want to be charged with drawing on my imagination when I have given the facts with respect to any one of these votes. There is a dwelling for the agent, which is necessary to have, and which will cost $1,000. There is also a station which is to cost $3,500 and grading and contingencies will cost $1,300, making $5,800. We have an appropriation for the current year of $3,500, leaving $2,300 to be voted for 1905-6.
Increased accommodation at Memr-amcook, $4,000.
There was a vote last year for this.
You are adding $3,000.

Yes, we asked $5,000 last year. I explained at that time that this was not the full cost of the station. We will expend in this year $3,000 and it is estimated that that will leave $2,000 of a revote, and we will require $2,000 more in order to complete the total work which will come to $7,000.
What is the nature of that work?

We have a new station and we are converting the old station into a freight shed, and we also require to do certain grading. There has been practically no freight accommodation there and the freight shed will cost $5,000. We have to buy some land there which will cost $200 and the grading will be $1,000.
You add that to the debt of the country?

It is an improvement;
a betterment. There are contingencies of $800, making a total of $7,000.

What would the revenue be
in a station of that size ?
It is a very important station.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: They all are.

Yes, in their own opiu-on they are; it is so represented. The revenue is" about $5,600. This is a large parisn and a growing station. They are developing oil fields in that section of New Brunswick and an oil refinery is now under construction not very far from the station.

I notice that the hon. minister has several votes for converting the present passenger stations into freight sheds.
Might I ask the minister if along the line of the Intercolonial, at places such as that under discussion, it is the policy to have the freight shed separate from the passenger station?
That is the policy. It would be impossible and it would be very poor economy indeed to have a freight shed as part of a station.
It is a very common thing.

It seems to me that where the revenue is less than $6,000 in prosperous years, a well constructed station with passenger station at one end and a freight station at the other would be all sufficient and would be very much more compact and very much better in the interest of the public than to have two separate buildings. I may be wrong about that, but in Ontario there are many stations of this kind at points where I am sure the revenue is very much in excess of $6,000 per annum. I was very much surprised to notice that the old shed is so often discarded and that we are now adopting the policy of converting passenger stations into freight sheds and erecting new passenger stations.

I notice that, there is no provision among these items for any improvement to the roadbed of the Canada Eastern Railway recently taken over by the government. Would the minister be good enough to state to the committee what the intentions of the department are with regard to the improvement of the roadbed of that line? I understand that when the minister proposed this purchase to the House last session he spoke glowingly of the earning prospects of the line, and intimated that if it were put in good condition and properly equipped it would pay. In the course of that discussion the hon. minister, questioned in the matter by one of the members from Toronto, said :-
It would not necessarily require to he up to the standard of the Intercolonial Railway, because it is not a trunk line and never will be. Without getting a report' from an engineer, I have been over the road and am satisfied that $1,000 a mile will make it a splendid, up-to-date road, and in my opinion this road, in the course of next year or so, will be worth $1,000,000, especially considering the situation of the government as regards the Fredericton bridge.
I would like to know if it is intended to take up this work to any extent during the present season ?

We have already been improving the Canada Eastern, paying out of revenue account. We have put in quite a number of sleepers, and that work will go on gradually. I made the statement last year that I believed $1,000 a mile, or about $100,000, would put that road in a condition to meet all the requirements. I

19S0
still stand by that. We are gradually improving it, but as it is paid for out of revenue, I do not ask any special vote. As to the necessities that may arise, X am not, at the moment, able to advise my hon. friend. The road now has better cars and engines and runs faster trains than before. This was done without great outlay because we could take from the Intercolonial Railway some of the smaller cars which are outclassed on the main line. In this way we are able to give the better service without material increase in the cost to the Railway Department.
Has the minister a report from an engineer showing what will be required to put the road in proper condition ?

A report was laid on the table last year ; covering report of the engineer on the roadbed and bridges, reports as to the mechanical outfit and general conditions for the road. That return, which was furnished when the matter was under discussion, will be found to contain all the information.
I understood from the passage I have quoted that the minister at that time had not the report of an engineer. If there is no report, is it intended to have one during the present season ?

If my remarks were made at the time the resolution was under discussion, there was a report of the engineer on the table of the House at that time. I was speaking about what I had gathered from going over the road.
The minister said a while ago that he did not know the population of this place St. Moise. Would he like to know it ? Has he not the latest report of the population of that place ?
I should be delighted to know it. I suppose I have the report, but it is not before me.
The minister would like to know it ? Well, the census report shows that there are 908 people in that parish- not in the village, but in the parish.

If the minister will allow us to go back for a moment I would like to refer to one of the details of this item of $135,800 for additional sidings and a spur line. That is an item of $18,000 for a spur track at Riviere Ouelle. 1 45-100 miles. This is at the rate of $12,000 a mile which is a fair estimate, perhaps, for a spur track. But, I find that while the hon. gentleman wants to spend $18,000 during the coming year on this spur track, he spent in the year ending June 30, 1904, $32,369. How much he has spent in the current year I do not know.
No, that was spent on the branch line running down to St. Denis wharf, the RiviCre Ouelle wharf.
He told us that this was a spur track at Riviere Ouelle.
Near Riviere Ouelle.
That is one of the difficulties we get into by the hon. gentleman coupling them all up.

I spoke of this spur track as west of Riviere Ouelle. The Ri-vi6re Ouelle branch is a short branch line connecting the Intercolonial Railway and the ferry wharf opposite Murray bay, a place that is frequented very largely by tourists. In the summer season we have a special sleeper which runs from Riviere Ouelle wharf through to Quebec with the American cities, so that tourists can get it at night.
How far is the new siding from that ?
It is over a mile west of Riviere Ouelle.
Then, the hon. gentleman is building two tracks, one costing over $32,000 and the other $18,000 ?
The Riviere Ouelle branch cost more than that.

That is the expenditure for one year. These two lines are within a mile of each other.
Now surely we ought to have an opportunity of criticising expenditures of that kind. Who is there in the province of Ontario or in the west who can possibly criticise the estimates without that knowledge? If we had these details-I am simply making an illustration of what we want-if we had these details, any gentleman in that district could have taken the minister's estimate of $18,000 for a spur track at Riviere Ouelle, and he would have seen that we had been already, within twelve months, spending $32,000 within a mile of it. That v\ ould have been subject for criticism. As it is, though the hon. gentleman introduced a general blanket resolution for $135,000, and asks us, because he has confidence in his officers who tell him that they want $135,000, to vote it without a word.
Subway near St. Fabien. S7.650.

This amount is required for a public road near St. Fabien station, which is located about 1,000 feet east of the station. There is a very steep bill there, and the people of that section coming down this steep hill are brought down to the track crossing, and. that track crossing is very near a large snow shed. It is a very dangerous crossing. The people cf that section sent in a petition representing the conditions, and I had them inquired

into by officers. They asked that the road, instead of stopping at the foot of this hill and crossing that track at a very dangerous point, should be extended onward where there is an embankment, and that there should be an under crossing, or a subway, built under the embankment, thus avoiding the dangers incident to that particular crossing. It crosses the railway at a point where everything is hidden from the approaching tiaveller until he is on the track.
! Mr. BARKER. Just like this item of 8125,000 whieh hides everything.
I congratulate the hon. gentleman on his apt remark. But the hiding in that case was unintentional, and the hiding at this station inevitable.

Going back to the previous item-in 1903-04 the hon. gentleman spent for a spur track at Riviere Ouelle 832,000, he is now asking to spend next year $18,000 at a siding which, he says, is a mile away from it. I do not know what i'.e has spent in the twelve months inter's ening between these two expenditures ; he may have expended $20,000 for aught we know. But how is it that we are expending a t .two places within a mile of each other so much money ? What is the reason for it?

The Riviere Ouelle spur line, as the hon. gentleman calls it, was not a spur line at all, it wras a branch line, VVe have an engine there connecting the Intercolonial with Murray Bay. An amount was voted for it by parliament two y ears ago, and the work was let by contract. Parliament also voted a sum of money for a large breakwater or wharf, which is made la landing pdace for a ferry. It is about a year and a half since that branch -was completed, and during the last two seasons it has been in operation as a branch of the Intercolonial. East year $32,000 was paid out in a final adjustment of the contract.
How much did the whole branch road cost ?
It was before my time. I do not bear it in mind.
What is the length ?
About seven miles.
You built a branch line of seven miles in length down to the St. Lawrence.

Yes, I think some call it Riviere Ouelle wharf, others oall it the St. Denis wharf. Now the people of Murray Bay are entirely shut out from any railway communication other than that afforded by lie Intercolonial and this ferry across the St. Lawrence. The Murray Bay people and Charlevoix people are shut out from railway communication. This year an attempt was made to keep the ferry open during the winter season so that the people on the
north shore of the St. Lawrence might have communication with the outside world.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: We want to know why the minister is building another spur within a mile of it, running down to the same Rivifire Ouelle.
No, this is a spur line in connection with the loading and gather ing up of lumber for the benefit of traffic on the Intercolonial. It is over a mile I think beyond Riviere Ouelle.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: What do you want the spur line there for ?
For the purposes of Intercolonial traffic.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: It is a mere siding on the Intercolonial, not a spur running out into the country ?	,
It is a spur siding, not a branch line.
Does it run to anybody's mill ?
Yes, Mr. Price has a n ill there, I think it runs to more than one mill. It is 1-45 miles long.

Did the minister say anything as to the increased traffic which has taken place over the road since the branch line has been built, and the wharf with whieh it connects ? I suppose the wharf was not built by the Intercolonial Railway.

I think the wharf was built some years ago, and that it has been there quite a number of years. It was not built by the Intercolonial Railway, but the Intercolonial Railway connects with it. It was a Public Works Department construction, and built quite a number of years ago for the benefit of the Riviere Ouelle people. They had packets running over there. Now they have steamers, and by reason of the fact that the Intercolonial Railway has made connection, the tourists that go to Murray Bay ate enabled to reach there much more quickly, and I think there has been quite an influx of traffic.

Will the hon. minister look that information up, and give us the total cost of the six miles and a statement as to the growth of traffic within the last two years ? What is the policy of the Intercolonial Railway in reference to branch spurs of a mile or a mile and a half or two miles in length ? For instance, I am a manufacturer and have a mill a mile or two from the railway ; I am anxious to get my products on to the road instead of hauling them by wagon or by sleigh, and I make application to the Intercolonial Railway to put in a spur-what is the policy of the railway in that respect ?

I am informed that the policy in connection with such sidings

is that the grading is done by the Intercolonial Railway and that the other parties pay so much for the rails.
The railway grade and the parties interested pay for the rails ?

Yes, they make some contribution. There is an arrangement reached between the parties. I think it is uniform and that it is open to all. I am not sufficiently acquainted with the details to make a definite statement as to this point.
Is that what has been done in this case ?
There has been a contribution, I think, in this case.

The hon. minister might look that up and give us that information too. There must be a general policy in connection with this work all through.
To increase accommodation at Amherst, $28,000.
What is this ?

This is in connection with the Amherst station and yard. The Intercolonial business at Amherst has grown with wonderful rapidity. The establishment of the car works there and quite a number of other kindred industries, the new foundry and machine shop and the enlargement of the Robb engineering works, together with a new woollen industry and several other establishments, which I cannot at the moment recall, have added very largely to the traffic of the Intercolonial Railway at that point The railway has under consideration the question of enlarging the yard and in some way improving the conditions as to the station accommodation. I do not know just exactly what form finally this will take. I was personally in company with the general manager, who was called to look over the situation, but as to how we can remedy it I am not in a position at this moment to say.
But some work has been done and some money has been expended ?

That was in the outside yards. We have extended the yards and sidings away out towards Nappan. There is such a congestion of streets and houses encroaching on the railway, and there was originally such an insufficient quantity of land reserved for the purposes of the railway, that it is now found necessary to have all the shunting sidings placed at a remote distance from the station. The increase in the number of trains has proved the necessity of an additional track. Quite a number of passenger trains meet there during the day, and we will certainly require an additional track at that point. But there is not width enough between the station and the car works of Messrs. Rhodes, Curry & Co., Limited, which are directly opposite. There is back of the sta-

tion quite a plot of land which belongs to the Intercolonial Railway. It has heretofore been utilized by the citizens of Amherst as a street, and the proposal is to have the station moved back on that plot in order to make it possible to have an additional track. We propose having, in that connection, umbrella sheds and a concrete platform. The traffic earnings of the Intercolonial Railway at that point, I think, last year were upwards of $280,000. I know there was a marvellous growth, and certainly the conditions would require some improvement.
How much is it proposed to expend ?
I am now asking for $28,000, of which $15,000 is a revote.
I know what you are asking for. How much is it proposed to expend ?
The total amount of the proposed expenditure is $44,000. It is estimated that $16,000 will be expended this year, leaving a balance of $28,000.

The hon. minister says that he does not know what he is going to
do.

To a certain extent.
I do not wish to be misunderstood by the committee. We propose double-tracking the line for 3,500 feet. There is no question as to that. We propose an improvement in the yards, and in the lumber yard connected with the station we propose an expenditure of $8,000. We require some large cattle pens, because of the maritime winter show being held there, a show such as they have in Guelph every year. That involves an expenditure of $1,000 ; and we want to improve the water service, which will cost $3,000 more. We want to have an engine-house, which will cost $1,500. We must keep a shunting engine at Amherst all the time in consequence of the increased business. The concrete platforms and sheds are estimated to cost somewhere in the vicinity of $5,000. As to what shall be done in connection with the station, it has not been determined, but of this $44,000, we have asked for $15,000 towards that.	_
That is not easy.

It is comparatively easy, but it will never be so easy again as it has been, so long as some of us here are members of the House. The minister will have had put through about $2,000,000 to-night, and the information concerning it is all contained on one page of this small book of the estimates. What has caused delay tonight, has been that those who have been criticising have been unable to get information. I hope that the minister next year will be able to tell us the expenditure on every siding and that he will set it down in the estimates together with the length of the siding, so that we may be able to know what the vote is asked for. Then there will be no delay. But to bring down an item for $132,000 and to oblige us to find out after two hours work that there are fifty or sixty different sidings scattered all over the whole Intercolonial, which are to be built out of that money, is the cause of a great deal of trouble. The minister would consult his own convenience and help us very much, if, in making out his estimates next year he would detail all these different things. Here we are with a railway which has a very large deficit, which has a very large capital expenditure, which has run the country into large expense already, and yet to listen to the minister asking for thousands of dollars for works all over the most settled parts of that road, one would almost come to the conclusion that the people have had no facilities for business in all these years, and that during the last year or two the minister had come to the conclusion that some sort of accommodation should be given to all these places. No one will dispute that there should be such accommodation as the business requires. What we would like to know is that the business of the place warrants the expenditure. What is the rule that the minister observes with reference to these ? I suppose requests come to him from the inhabitants of the different places ?
From boards of trade and town councils and members of parliament. I had a conference with the board of trade at Amherst for instance.

All these are legitimate sources whence these requests should come, but after all the requests are in I suppose the minister has reports from his officers w'ho take into account traffic considerations only as a basis. In some cases it would be well for us to have these reports so that we may see just what the officers -who are always non-partisan and look towards the traffic of the railroad rather than anything 63
else, recommend with regard to these different things.
Semaphores at stations, $1,000.

Has it occurred to the minister that he is seriously asking parliament to grant him 60 cents a mile on the Intercolonial for semaphores ; a railway that has been in operation for fifty years ? ' Does he realize that he is charging this to capital account?- Surely that is running the capital account mad. It is an outrage that this item should be put on the estimates as a charge against the capital of the country. The line must be drawn somewhere, and I ask the minister to strike out this item. If it Is not withdrawn I shall take some opportunity on concurrence, or at some other time, to have a vote of the House on this question.

These are semaphores at stations where they have never had them before. The railroad must be increased in value to that extent, and as such it is a betterment. This is a vote that goes on year after year. It is not replacing something, but it is creating something that has never been on the railway.

A few years ago I found an instance where a bucket at one of the intercolonial stations had been charged to capital account. Somebody wanted to do some whitewashing with the idea of improving the station, and so a water bucket was added to the debt of Canada. This vote Is something on a par with that. I shall take the sense of the House on the question as to whether that sort of thing is capital expenditure or not.
Would not the hon. gentleman draw a distinction In the case of absolutely new semaphores
It was a new bucket too.

I do not remember about the bucket, but there is a distinction between a new semaphore erected for a new station and a semaphore erected to replace an old one which originally had been charged to capital.
Supposing there were a ton of axle grease required on the railroad more in 1905 than in 1906. would that be charged to capital account ?
There is no analogy.

It runs much easier.
Hollins stock, $698,500.

I would ask the minister to allow this item to stand until he gives the House the information which I asked for this afternoon, namely, the expenditure on capital account on the Intercolonial Railway from 1896, and previous to that date if he wishes, the amount of rolling stock that has been charged to capital account since 1896, with the amount of rolling stock that



was in use in 1890 and the amount that is in use now, and the number of engines and cars under the various classifications. We cannot discuss this item without that information.

And in addition to that, the rolling stock that was not in a proper state of repair on the 30th of June last, and on the 1st of January last.
Intercolonial Railway-improving grades on line, $2-2,000.

This is to improve the grades on the line between Daveluyville and St. Wenceslas. In connection with this work it will be necessary to build two arch culverts. The grades will be improved at two points. At one point, two miles west of Daveluyville, two reverse grades of 1 per cent-one 600 feet long, the other 700 feet long-will be taken out, and the track made level. A bridge of 21 feet span will be replaced with a 10-feet arch culvert. At the other point, one quarter mile west of St. Wenceslas, two reverse grades-one 0"75 per cent, 1,000 feet long, the other 1T2 per cent, 100 feet long-will be replaced by 1,000 feet of level track and 1,000 feet of a 1 per cent grade. A bridge of 25-feet span will be replaced with a 16-feet arch culvert.
Intercolonial Railway-extension to Sydney Mines, $50,000.

This is to connect the Intercolonial with Sydney Mines from the
landing at North Sydney. Sydney Mines has recently forged ahead, the Nova Scotia Steel Company having enlarged its works there.
What is the distance ?
It is about two and three quarter miles.
Is all the expense being borne by the country ?
Yes.
The usual custom, where a railway builds a siding to a mine or a mill, is for the mill owners or mine owners to put up the money.
Sydney Mines is a large town. It has a mayor and all the modern equipment of a town. Its population is about 7,000.

As the minister mentioned Sydney Mines and the works of the Nova Scotia Steel Company, I thought the extension was to its mines. At any rate, what I say applies to several of these items. The usual custom is to require those who want a siding put in to a mine or a mill to deposit the money or pay a part of the cost, which is rebated to them from freight ; so that the railway company Is not out of pocket if the enterprise is not a paying concern Mr. OSLER.
to the railway. I think that plan ought to be adopted by the Intercolonial Railway absolutely. If not, pressure is likely to be brought to bear, from political interest, to have lines built to mills or mines that will never pay the cost. .
Has North Sydney anything to do with this extension ?

No. This is two miles or a little over beyond North Sydney.
Intercolonial Railway-steel rails and fastenings, $380,000.
Where is that to be expended ?
We obtained last year $495,000, and it is estimated that this $380,000 will provide for the laying of 200 more miles of the Intercolonial Railway with the heavier rails.
The cost of new rails is how much ?
The cost at the present place would be upwards of $30 per ton.
This is only the difference between the cost of the new rails and the value of the old rails as taken up, as the minister stated this afternoon.
Yes.
How many tons of rails is this going to supply ?
About 25,000 tons.
That is $750,000, or at $2S per ton, $700,000. The minister is asking $380,000 for it.
I am putting in the total of SO pound rails and fastenings which include the angle plates, bolts, nuts and tie plates. The total is $822,415.49.
That includes the fastenings without labour ?
The labour is provided out of revenue.
There is no doubt about that ?

So I am informed by the engineer who ought to know. I know that in tlie estimate before me there is no charge for labour. This is, less the credit of the rails that are taken up as well as the angle plates and nuts, $442,490. This leaves a balance of $379,925.45 which for greater case we call $380,000.
Then you are charging the bolts and fastenings to capital ; there is no allowance for the old bolts and nuts.
We are allowing for the old ones taken up.
If the minister was taking up a 66 pound rail and replacing it with a new 66 pound rail how would he charge it?
If the old rail were entirely worn out it would perhaps be properly charged to capital account. I do not know the custom, I have not had that particular phase of the question presented to me.
But the hon. gentleman (lias been in the House for three or four years when this very question was being discussed.
Oh that is hypothetical.

No, it is a practical question. If the hon. gentleman were replacing 66 pounds of old scrap rail with 66 pounds of new rail, the whole expense would be borne by his revenue. Why does he charge 80 pounds when he is only putting in, and actually improving his track, by 14 pounds of rail.
We give credit for the 66 pounds.
That is scrap.
It is not worn out, we sell it for $20 a ton.

But the hon. gentleman knows that the charges are all alike. If he takes up 20 pounds of old rail a large portion of it must be scrap as on every railway. Some of it may be good and may be sold as second-hand rail. I believe that some of it is placed on the Prince Edward Island Railway and some of it sold, but a large part of it must be scrap. The hon. gentleman puts in an additional weight of 14 pounds and instead of charging to capital only this 14 pounds he charges the whole 80 pounds to capital and gives a credit only for the scrap. The hon. gentleman knows perfectly well and Mr. Pottinger his general manager will tell him, that he makes money and improves his revenue at the expense of capital by every 80 pound rail he puts in. When I asked Mr. Pottinger the year before last whether as a railway man he considered he was justified in charging the 80 pound rail to capital, his answer was : Why should I not do so if parliament votes the money ?

We are asking a vote to relay the Intercolonial Railway with 80 pound rails. We are taking up the lighter class of rail and for the 200 miles taken up we allow $20 per ton. The difference is therefore a charge against capital account.
What is the weight of the present rails-66 pounds ?
We are taking up 67 pound rails.
If the minister went into the market for 67 pound rails what would he pay per ton ?

I presume he would pay the same price per ton. There is very little difference between the heavier and the lighter rails. I think, according to quotations which I have seen recently, they are practically the same.
What would be the proportion of mileage which the two classes of rails would lay?
We are simply charging for the 200 miles that we have laid down. For the 80 pound rail the tonnage per mile is 125 -7 tons to the mile and for the 67 pound rail 105'2 tons to the mile.

I understand that the minister proposes to lay about 200 or 250 miles of rail for which he will pay about $700,000. Last year he laid 161 miles of rail. Will he give us an idea of the cost of the 110-pound rail he laid ?

These were special rail, purchased from the Ghignecto Marine Railway Company, a rail that was brought to Canada for the purpose of the ship railway. The Intercolonial purchased them last year, I believe. I am not personally familiar with the transaction, as it took place before I had any connection with the department.
Do we understand that the minister has a big stock of these rails on hand ?
They are all laid.

The only amount that ought to be charged to capital account in this connection is for the increased weight of the new rail. The track was there, laid with 67-pound rails, which are replaced with 80-pound rails. There can be no increased value except in the increased cost of the heavier rails. The minister says that for these 250 miles, he will buy 25,000 tons at $28 a ton, which will amount to $700,000. He gives credit at the rate of $20 a ton for rails that are replaced. They are less cost -they would be lighter. Twenty dollars a ton for twenty-five thousand tons would amount to $500,000, and the difference between that and $700,000 is $200,000. There is no possible excuse even on the minister's own statement for charging to capital account more than this difference. The minister is taking $380,000, which means that $180,000 is an absolute mis-eharge, and, to that extent, his statement is misleading. That $180,000 should come out of the earnings of this railway as submitted to the House. There is no excuse ; no explanation can be made ; it is an absolute falsification, so far as the revenue and expenditure of the railway is concerned, if these figures are allowed to go through and this sum to be charged to the capital expenditure of the railway.
This is the course that has always been pursued

Not at all.
Mr. EM'MERSON. I beg the hon. gentleman's pardon

I beg the hon. gentleman's pardon. I went into that three years ago. Hon. Mr. Blair made that assertion and I proved by producing the reports that under Hon. Mr. Haggart not only was no amount charged to capital that might not properly be so charged, but he charged to revenue even the increased weight of the rail, which he was not obliged to do.

My information is
that that was the rule, as applied to the Intercolonial. Whether there were such replacements of rails as far back as Hon. Mr. Haggart's day, I do not know.
When the hon. minister says that was the rule
I say it has been the lule on the Intercolonial Railway.
Under Hon. Mr. Blair ?
And before Mr. Blair's time I believe.
That was refuted absolutely.

My information is different-I cannot speak of the matter personally. My hon. friend (Mr. Barker) makes the statement the other way. I am bound to accept his statement, but I can also rely, I think, upon the information given to me ; and that information is that this is the rule. I do not know what the rule is on other railways. My hon. friend from West Toronto (Mr. Osier) is a director of the Canadian Pacific Railway, I believe, and would know what the rule is on that road. That company may not have been laying the heavier rails for many years, and perhaps are not put to the question of how to make this charge.

The minister, I think, will know that I have always had a great reluctance in speaking on any subject in this House, to back up my opinions by saying what the Canadian Pacific Railway or any other company had done. I have great reluctance in mixing up with the discussions here, knowledge which may be said to come to me personally. But I may say that I do not believe there is a railway on this continent that, if it had an item like this before it would charge to capital as much as I am suggesting now should be charged-the difference between the weight of the rail taken up and that of the rail which replaces it.

I would add that if the minister will look into the question, he will find that in the first year of Mr. Blair's Mr. OSLER.
administration of the Intercolonial, he charged this item of steel rails just as Hon. Mr. Haggart, his predecessor, had been charging it, and as we say it ought to be charged. It was afterwards that Mr. Blair changed his system, and began to save his revenue by charging expenditures up to the debt of the country that should have been paid out of ordinary working expenses.

The statement made by my hon. friend from West Toronto (Mr. Osier) was a very strong and very clear statement. If that statement is correct, and if the basis, the arrangement laid down by the minister himself is correct, that all that is to be charged is the added cost, then the two corroborate each other ; and if these two be true, the practice of the minister, as exemplified by the vote he is asking here to-night, is dead against both these positions. Then the minister falls back on the assertion that it has been the practice to filch-there is no other name for it-from capital in order to save the appearance of a deficit or diminishing of the revenue. He say's it has been the practice in the Railway Department. Now, we want to know the facts in that case. Has it been the practice to do that ? How long has it been the practice to do that, and is the statement that my hon. friend from Hamilton (Mr. Barker) makes a true statement or not, that it was not the practice under the Minister of Railways of the previous government ? I think this is a very important matter. It has been talked of in this House in committee over and over again every year, and I think we have come to a point now where we must insist that attention should be given to it, and I think it is better that this item should stand to-night. The minister can inform himself from his department, he can take the time to do so, and give us the information, and let us come down to an honest and proper basis for making our estimates as regards capital and revenue. Now, if the minister will do that, we will get at least what was the practice of the department. He has an idea that it was so and so ; he is not supposed to know exactly what has been going on there all the time, because he is new to his position ; but he has officers who can give him that information, and a little search would enable him to state authoritatively on that point. This is a striking ease. Now, let us know what we are going to do in the future. I, for one, have a strong opinion that we ought to make honest estimates, no matter where the deficiency falls.

The facts are entirely before the House. It might be interesting to know, as a matter of research, what had been done in the past. I know that last year the item of $495,000 was voted in this particular way. I have followed the precedent established at that time so far as I am concerned. In the previous year, when

the estimates went through, the present Minister of Finance was the acting Minister of Railways. At that time there was a discussion the same as at present. There is no misunderstanding as to the application of the vote. Everybody knows for what purpose the money is asked and the circumstances under which it is expended. It seems to me that, under these conditions, this vote should pass as it is now. So far as I am personally concerned, I shall certainly take into consideration the features of the case presented by my hon. friend, who speaks with knowledge of what the Canadian Pacific Railway and other railways do. There is one thing about it; according to the views I hold with respect to the Intercolonial, I am quite prepared to insist that every dollar should be rightly placed. I am not afraid of the items appearing in the revenue charge if it is proper to place them there, and I do not want to put them in capital account if they do not belong there. Those are the views I hold. But this course was followed last year ; there was not a very full discussion, certainly not so full as we have had to-night. I would ask that this vote be allowed to go as it is, and, so far as I am concerned and have anything to do with the matter in the future, I shall deal with it from the standpoint of inquiring into the actual facts. I am sure I shall be borne out, not only by my friends opposite, but by our friends on this side.

The minister has been frank, and, so far as he has stated his position, it is satisfactory to the committee. But here is the point with me. Has the minister himself any doubt at all that upon this single item which is now under discussion the facts of the case are as stated by my hon. friend from Toronto (Mr. Osier) ? Has he the least doubt in the world that he is asking for capital to do more than to replace the road in the exact position it was in before ? Now, he has an answer to that or he has not. If his answer is that it appears from that reasoning and from the facts that he is taking from capital to run the road, then I think he is bound to take the matter into consideration and make his decision before this passes, no matter what the practice has been in the past. We ought to stop the very moment we are agreed that the practice is as bad as it has been proved to be in this particular instance. The minister would not ask us to give him a sum on capital account for the payment of his conductors, for the payment of his bills for coal for running the road, or for anything else than that which went absolutely into running expenses. Now, here is an item which runs up into the hundreds of thousands of dollars, in which, on a showing which is incontest-ible and as to which there has been no answer, he is taking about $200,000 out of icapital and is throwing it into the running-expenses of the road, taking $200,000 off this
vote, and the minister is able to put on heavier rails in place of lighter ones, and have his roadbed, his track and everything just as it was before, and the difference between the cost of the two is all that he ought to take out of capital for that purpose. Surely there does not seem to be any doubt about that. Although we acknowledge the fairness with which the minister has met us, yet I believe it would be better for him to allow this to stand and to make up his mind with reference to the principle. It is no disparagement at all to a minister, when he finds that he is asking for something that he ought not properly to ask for, and if, after looking into it, he finds that it is not the right way, no matter what others have done, to say that he proposes to do what is correct in the matter from this time on, and not to step off a $200,000 platform of error on to his platform of true and honest estimates that he is going to rear after this particular vote is through, I want the minister to understand that this is a matter which I think is vital. We might just as well take our stand upon it and fight it out now on both sides of the House as to have it going on and being a perennial sore from year to year. I think the minister agrees with me in that respect, that he ought to make honest estimates.

I certainly agree with my hon. friend that we should make honest estimates, but I am not convinced that the statement of the hon. member for Toronto (Mr. Osier) is correct as to the way in which these estimates should be prepared. Now, it seems to me, from my standpoint at least, that in this instance, where an allowance is made for rails, and there is a difference in their value, as respects the worn rails, a sufficient allowance is borne by revenue, and the difference of the $380,000 should be borne by capital.
The hon. minister is shifting his ground.

There is no deception in respect to the matter. It is quite apparent on the face of it as to what is to be done, as to the actual facts and circumstances of the whole transaction and one can form a judgment in respect to them. It seems to me that as it stands the cost of the 80 pound rail, less the credit of the other rail, is a fail-charge against capital account.

Suppose that the hon. minister could not sell these 67-lb. rails that he has taken up for more than $10 a ton, would he consider it right to take the difference between $10 and $28, calculating it out as we have calculated it here to-night, and charge that to capital? Suppose he could not sell these rails for more than $5 a ton, would he consider it right to do that? Suppose he could not sell them for a dollar a ton, that they went just as scrap and poor at that, would he consider it right to take the

balance out of capital? Why could be not sell them for more than $10 or $5 a ton? Simply because they had been worn out in the service of the railway. When he was putting on new rails what is he doing? He is making provision for worn out stuff and provision for worn out stuff must be borne by the current revenue of the railway and not by capital. There cannot be any escape from that reasoning, surely. We are not trying to make arguments one against the other and seeing who will get the best of it. That is not it. We are trying to come at the truth. Why do you sell these old rails at $20, for I am coming to the hon. minister's own price? You sell them at $20 because they have been on the Intercolonial Railway for a number of years, they are worn and they are not worth more than $20. They have been worn in the service of the road. The service of the road has been to produce revenue and the hon. minister is replacing what was worn in the service of the road to produce revenue by getting capital to put a good rail in the place of the worn out rail. It seems to me so clear that the hon. minister must see it, as I think he does see it, and as I think we all will see it. If that be true, it is absolutely wrong-I am not going to say dishonest-to take capital to till that gap.

With the hon. minister's last word before he sat down I agree most thoroughly. He sat down with a statement that the difference between the cost of the new rail and the price of the old rail should be charged to capital. I agree with that Taking his figure of $20 as the value of the rail and his figure of $28 as the cost of the new rail, that is $200,000, which, according to that contention, should be charged to capital. But the minister is asking for a charge of $380,000. The hon. minister says there is no dishonesty at all-I do not for a moment suggest such a thing, but if that statement goes out in connection with the Intercolonial, and this is one of many items, the fact remains absolutely that there is a false statement in so far as the earnings and revenue of the intercolonial are concerned to the extent of $180,000 in this one item. I am speaking only of it being a false statement in the sense that It is incorrect bookkeeping and that it conveys a false impression to the public in respect to that $180,000. It ought to be charged to revenue and not to capital, and if this item goes through then the Intercolonial statement for next year will be false to the extent of the amount which I have mentioned in this one item alone.
Would the hon. minister state what contracts for rails have been closed during the past year with the Lake Superior corporation and what deliveries have taken place?

Two contracts with the Sault Ste. Marie Company, the first given in September for 10,000 tons and another in October, I think, for 10,800 tons more, were entered into. Twenty-eight thousand tons have been delivered. There have been ao othei contracts entered into or arranged.
What were the prices of these rails?

The prices were to be fixed by the open market price plus the duty. The open market price, I think, on the 1st October was to govern the first 10,000 and the open market price on the 15th November was to govern as to the delivery of the 10,800 tons.
Could the hon. minister state what amounts have been paid for these tails or if they have yet determined the actual cost of them?
That has not yet been determined. There -was an amount paid them pro rata on the advice of the chief engineer pending the decision. The decision was to be made by the Minister of Railways and Canals.
What was the amount that was paid?

I think it was $23 a ton, but I will not be certain. At any rate there was a large margin reserved to protect the department, and I am endeavouring to get information from standard dealers in England as to the actual sales in order that I may determine the prices that ruled on the 1st October and 15th November last respectively.
Were these the dates that were to govern the price?

I know the last was the 15th November. I am quite positive also that the first was the 1st of October, but 1 speak subject to correction. I am quite certain, however, the first was the 1st of October.
What other contracts for rails for the Intercolonial hare been closed?
No other contracts have been entered into other than these two.
I mean with any other companies or individuals. I am not speaking only of the Lake Superior Company.
These are the only contracts that have been entered into by the Intercolonial.
The hon. minister did not state at what points the new rails are to he laiu down during the coming summer on the Intercolonial Railway.

On the eastern division about three-quarters of a mile ; between St. John and Shediac about sixty-two miles,

and the balance of the hundred miles between Moncton and Levis.
I would ask the minister to allow the item to stand until he will be kind enough to give us the information with reference to what has been the practice in the department.
Could not the item be passed in the meantime ?
I do not think we will ever get a simpler or a clearer point on which to take up our respective positions than this is, and no time will be wasted by allowing the item to stand.
I have no desire to rush the items through.

Let me remark here that the statement made by the Minister of Railways last evening in reference to the Intercolonial was one of the most doleful and discouraging I ever heard a Minister of Railways make in this House. In view of the method pursued at the present time of charging to capital account, items which should be charged to revenue, the statement of the minister was even more doleful than would appear on the surface. I listened very attentively to the hon. gentleman and I regret that while he gave several excuses for the immense deficit, he failed to' suggest a remedy. I disagree entirely with the statement of the minister, that it matters very little to the country whether items are charged to capital or to revenue, because the people have to pay them anyway. It is all very well for members of this House on both sides who fully understand the situation, but the people generally have not the advantages we have here, and they are consequently not in a position to judge of the merits of the management of the Intercolonial. The minister evidently wants to be honest in the matter ; I give him the credit that he evidently is not trying to hide anything. While I have always been in favour of government ownership of railways I have always held that the management of our government railways was not conducted on proper principles. I say now as I have often said before, that I do not accuse the Liberal party any more than I have accused my own party, with improper management of our railways. It does not make any difference how competent your general manager may be, there is too much interference with him to permit him to manage the railroad properly. Every officer on our government railways is being interfered with from time to time by politicians and others, and in consequence of that interference they are not allowed to use their judgment and their experience as they otherwise would. It is because of that interference that the people of Canada are called upon year after year to make up by indirect taxation enormous deficits on the Intercolonial. Let me say here
