that the Minister of Railways would do a good thing if he were to keep the accounts of the government railways ns other railway corporations keep their accounts. If he did that he would show the people of Canada that under the present system of management large annual deficits cannot be prevented, and public feeling would be so stirred that a demand would come from the people of Canada for a change. If the government railways were taken out of the sphere of political interference and placed, say under control of a properly constituted commission, I feel satisfied that they would be an asset of which our country might be proud. I have had experience in supporting a government in this House years ago, and I know that members are frequently called upon to do certain things for their constituents which in their own good judgment should not be done. If our government railways were placed entirely under control of a commission, the supporters of the government would be relieved of this unpleasant task, and in their interest as well as in the interest of the country the outcome would be beneficial. I am not criticising our government railways in any carping spirit. I realize that we have 1,400 or 1,500 miles of government railways in Canada, and that the more politics is kept out of the management, the better it is for all concerned. I trust that the minister will bring down the information asked for to-night. I for one wilLhold up both hands in support of the minister, if he carries out that policy. I tell him that if he endeavours to control the government railways in the interest of the people of the country and in as economical a manner as possible he will be supported by public opinion.

I court the fullest criticism of the management of the Intercolonial, so long as that criticism is based upon facts and not upon any political or partisan motives. I recognize that the Intercolonial by reason of the circumstances that surround it, has reached a time in its history when it certainly demands the earliest consideration of the people of the country.
Hear. hear.

I recognize that. I recognize the fact that there are two or three very large corporations that are looking with longing eyes on the Intercolonial, and I think i can also recognize the fact that it is a question between, and among, these corporations as to how' the spoil is to be divided. I also recognize that anything that can be said in this House or before the country to the discredit of government management of the Intercolonial will only serve to improve the prospects of these corporations ; and, without mentioning the particular cor-operations. I can quite understand why it *would be in their interest that the people of this country should be educated up to

the point of condemning every transaction in connection with the Intercolonial. Now, notwithstanding all this, notwithstanding the fact that I see the dangers ahead, I am quite prepared, as Minister of Railways, to have the whole situation exposed to the gaze of the public. I am met saying this in any heroic way, but I am speaking of it as a necessity in the interest of the road itself. If there are difficulties which are within the control of the department, those difficulties should be grappled with. I have endeavoured to point out, in a non-partisan spirit, difficulties which I believe exist and over which I think we could not have any control. I endeavoured, in my statement last night, to present the actual facts, and to show that in almost every instance in which there was a deficit, the expenditure was beyond the control of the department-such as the extra wages, the repairs to rolling stock, and the purchase of rolling stock out of revenue. My hon. friend from Hamilton has said that the conditions of the Intercolonial in this respect are much better to-day than they were on a previous occasion.

They ought to be, too.
Mr. E'MMERSON. So they ought to be ; I grant it ; the extent to which they ought to be is demonstrated by the extra expenditure in the working expenses during the past year and the current six months. With regard to the book-keeping, how long that has prevailed on the Intercolonial, I am not prepared to say. If you compare this year with last year or with the last four or five years, you find the same conditions. How far back they go I do not know ; nor dr- I know whether there was any occasion ir< the years gone by to substitute a heavier 'or a lighter rail. For the reason stated, I am quite prepared to have the information with reference to this item brought before the House. I have given the reason why I think this vote should be passed ; but, in deference to the views expressed, I am quite willing that it should stand in the meantime.

In answer to what the hon. gentleman has said, I admit that the roiling stock is in a better condition ; why should it not be ? For years under the present government we hg.ve been voting enormous sums of money to buy new rolling stock. During the year 1903-04 we paid 55043,000 for new rolling stock ; for the current year the hon. gentleman took a vote of 551,000,000 for the same purpose, and as he is not seeking a revote of that, I presume he is spending it.
What I said was that with respect to the rolling stock that has been purchased out of revenue, we are in a better position than we would have been last year.

I admit that ; but under what pressure from this side of the House has that been accomplished ? For four Mr. EMMERSON.
years we protested against the fact that year after year the government were allowing greater numbers of cars to fall into disuse, to go on to the dump heap, until in the beginning of last year they had 55S cars of dead stock on their hands. We pointed out 1hat while the government in order to save their working expenses, neglected to repair these cars, they were spending millions in buying new rolling stock on capital account. At present the hon. gentleman is asking $698,000 more for rolling stock, although he is rather boastfully saying now that the rolling stock is in a good condition. I do not know whether.the hon. gentleman is going to ask us for anything more. East year I think we had about four supplementary votes before we got through. But surely, under such circumstances, the rolling stock should improve. Now, let me say this about the Intercolonial Railway. We have criticised its management. We want the Intercolonial to get a fair chance to show what is in it. We want the officers and the staff of the Intercolonial to have the same chance as the officers and the staff of every other railway in this country ; and I believe that if the official staff of the Intercolonial had bad that freedom from interference on the part of politicians that railway companies have, there would have been a very different result, in the earnings el the line. We are not despondent. I do not know whether the hon. gentleman has any reason for despondency with regard to the Intercolonial Railway. We used to hear the hon. Minister of Finance and other ministers boast of the brilliant prospects of that railway under present auspices ; but since about a year ago we have been hearing a very different tale from them. The hon. gentlemen who used to boast of this railway are now becoming despondent-why? Are they crying stinking fish ? Are they trying to get rid of the railway ? Is there some applicant for it in the market ? How is it that the men who a few years ago were so boastful of this line, are now so despondent that the minister yesterday made a speech that was characterized on this side of the House as the most despondent ever uttered with regard to this railway ? That is the position we take ; we believe that this railway ought to have a fair show. In the last four years every railway in Canada has been almost over-burdened with traffic. The Grand Trunk Railway and the Canadian Pacific Railway have been earning enormous sums above their working expenses. The government railway alone has been a burden. We say :	Give the staff of the
Intercolonial the same freedom, the same opportunities that are enjoyed by the staffs of the Grand Trunk Railway and the Canadian Pacific Railway, and under proper management freed from political interference and officialism the results would be very different from what they are and what they have been.

Before you pass from this item, Mr. Chairman, there are one or two things I desire to say in answer to the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat (Mr. Barker) and to the hon. member for Elgin (Mr. Ingram). They have been pleased to criticise the statement of the Minister of Railways yesterday as the most doleful ever presented to this House. The people throughout this country, but more particularly the workmen along the line of the Intercolonial who are a very important class of people in this country will not criticise that statement as the most doleful ever presented to this parliament. They will regard it as the happiest statement for them and therefore for the country'that has ever been presented by a Minister of Railways. The Minister of Railways nas been able to say that for the first time in the history of the country he has been able to do justice to the men employed on the Intercolonial. Time was-and those of us who live on the line of the Intercolonial remember it very well-when the workmen on the Intercolonial appealed to former Ministers of Railways and appealed In vain that justice might be done to them. There never was a time in the history of the Intercolonial Railway when the officials of the road were so free from interference from politicians and others as at the present time. I want to call to the mind of the hon. melhber for Hamilton (Mr. Barker) jhls fact that if he seeks to know what has been transpiring with respect to it he would do' well to consult with the officials on the Intercolonial who were there previous to 1896 ; he would learn where the interference came from in those days. That was the day when shingles were being issued all over tne Intercolonial Railway. The line was more noted for the purpose of carrying shingles in 1896 than for any other purpose.
It is hay now.

My hon. friend says it is hay. Yes, very true, and he will find that those responsible for the management of the Intercolonial Railway will be in a position to go before the people of this country and justify to the full their conduct in connection with the carrying of hay.
The have not done so.

We will be prepared to go with the hon. member for East Simcoe to the people of this country and to justify our conduct in this connection. We will take issue with our friends opposite on this question as we have on every other question in connection with the Intercolonial Railway since 1896. I tell my hon. friends opposite that they do not know the conditions that prevail along the Intercolonial Railway to-day. I believe what is more that they do not know the conditions that obtained along the Intercolonial Railway previous to 1896. The men who were 64
ashamed of the Intercolonial Railway then, when it was in the hands of hon. gentlemen opposite are to-day prepared to go before the people of this country and to say that they are proud of the Intercolonial Railway to-day. Was there any one in this country who was proud of the Intercolonial Railway during the days when it was administered by our hon. friends opposite ? I want to know if there is one member on the opposite side who is prepared to stand in his place to-night and say that previous to 1896 the Intercolonial Railway under Conservative administration was creditable to the people of this country. Is there one among them to-day prepared to deny the fact that the Intercolonial Railway to-day is a credit to the people of this country ? The Minister of Railways told the House yesterday that it was not the purpose of the Intercolonial Railway from the time it was started to make money for the people of Canada. He said truly, and I support the statement in its entirety, that the Intercolonial Railway ought to be regarded, has been regarded, and will continue to be regarded as a complete-n ent of the canal system of this country. Those of us who live along the line of the Intercolonial are not whining and complaining day after day about the moneys that are being spent by the people in maintaining the efficiency of the canal system of this country. We regard it as important to the people of Ontario that the canal system should be maintained in its efficiency, and we are not going before the people and complaining that the money is being wasted and squandered upon them. For live years I have sat in this House and listened to a former Minister of Railways complaining, about tile money that was being spent upon this road. Member after member sitting opposite told the people that it was idle to wraste money on the Intercolonial Railway, that it was to be a sinkhole for the money of the people of this country and still they are not satisfied. Who was it that tried to dispose of the Intercolonial Railway ? My hon. friend from Hamilton (Mr. Barker) a few moments ago expressed a fear that the present Minister of Railways and the present government were desirous of parting with it. Who are the only political party in this country that ever tried to dispose of the Intercolonial Railway ? Let them read the record of their party previous to 1896, and they will find that they were prepared to hand over to the Canadian Pacific Railway this Intercolonial Railway. Who was it that did everything possible to cripple the services of the Intercolonial Railway ? Who was it that entered into a contract with the Canadian Pacific Railway to render practically useless to the maritime provinces and the people of this country the Intercolonial Railway ? Let them call to mind the agreement, entered into by the former Conservative administration of the Intercolonial with the Canadian Pacific Railway. The Liberal



party has been found fault with by hon. gentlemen because it was thought desirable in the interest , of the people of this country, but more particularly in the interests of those served by the Intercolonial, to cancel that agreement. For my own part X have nothing but admiration for the management of the Intercolonial Railway since 1890. i am prepared to go before my own people and I am quite sure that every member on this side of the House is prepared to go before his constituents and defend the management of the Intercolonial Railway since 1890. I say that there have been deficits on the Intercolonial Railway [DOT], these deficits are not new, they existed in former times and I have no doubt that they will continue to exist. I do not know whether they will ever be avoided, but I do know that the people of this country are getting good value for them, are getting much better value to-day for the present deficits of the Intercolonial Railway than they did for those that existed before 1896. The people are given a good service to-day. It remained to the Intercolonial Railway since 1896, it remained to the present government to raise the standard of the railway travel in this country. They set the example and other roads have been obliged to raise the standard of their travel and the comfort of their passengers and therefore it is that all sections of this country, but more particularly those sections traversed by the Intercolonial Railway, are prepared to defend in all respects the management and administration of the Railway Department from 1896 to the present time.

One remark was 'made by the hon. gentleman (Mr. A. Johnston), who has just taken his seat, which, I think, is not exactly correct. He stated that, so far as he knows, every railway official on the Intercolonial-which, I suppose, would include the Prince Edward Island Railway -was left free from political influence. 1 wish to tell this House that at the last election on the 3rd of November last, a large number of Conservative officials on the Prince Edward Island Radway were handed the book and the briberv oath were put to them. I ask whether that is political influence or not ? I ask whether that is freedom or not ? I think the statement made by the hon. gentleman is not borne out by the facts. He has made another statement-that the people of the maritime provinces are satisfied with the Intercolonial Railway as it is conducted to-day. But if you will remember the statement made by the minister yesterday, he told us that he was unable to carry the grain from the west to Halifax and St.
John, because he had not' sufficient rolling stock. At the same time, these gentlemen put upon the statute-book a la .v which provides that the money of the people of Canada shall be used in the construction of another road paralleling the Intercolonial and taking away the traffic that ought to go to that road. If the Intercolonial Railway today is deficient in rolling stock to carry the grain from the west to the ports which they boast so much about as the winter ports of this country, why is not the public money used to put this road in a proper state to carry this business instead of wasting it in constructing a road to be handed over to the Grand Trunk Pacific that they may carry the grain to the foreign port of Portland? I think that when these hon. gentlemen say that this road is in efficient condition, they do not speak by the book. They boast of the increase of wages. I have no fault to find with them for the increase of the wages if they have the money to do it. But they have not the revenue, because they have not the trafiic, and they say they have not the traffic because they have not the means of carrying it. But when did they raise the salaries of the officials ? Immediately before the election of 3rd of November last. The Minister of Railways (Mr. Emmerson) went down to Moncton some time in October. Conferences were held at the office in Moncton. Delegations were there from every department in the Intercolonial Railway to- meet the minister-that is reported in the public press, at any rate. Arrangements were made at that time for the increase of wages all round, with the exception of the staff in the accountant's department of the railway.
How many increases in wages were there before that ?
Perhaps the hon. gentleman (Mr. A. Johnston) can tell. At any rate, these increases were made at the time when the government party required the votes of the officials of the railway.
